items.title: fix(benchmarks): correct eight measurement bugs and share the harness
items.body:
Acts on a review of the benchmark system. I verified every claim against the real code before applying anything, and **A/B'd the whole change on real hardware** — same benchmark, real headed Chrome and Firefox, before and after.

## The A/B result: the harness change does not move the measurements

| | median \|Δ\| | max \|Δ\| |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chrome | **0.3%** | 33% (one arm, see below) |
| Firefox | **0.3%** | 9.4% |

The headline metric — stream skip % — moved at most **1.6pp across 8 arms, 5 of them exact**:

```
arm                       old skip%  new skip%    Δpp
prose/20/always                91.7       91.7   +0.0
prose/20/onDemand              91.7       91.7   +0.0
prose/50/always                79.1       77.5   -1.6
prose/50/onDemand              79.1       79.1   +0.0
code/20/always                 91.5       91.4   -0.1
code/20/onDemand               91.2       91.5   +0.3
code/50/always                 75.7       74.6   -1.1
code/50/onDemand               77.3       77.5   +0.2
```

The one 33% outlier was `prose/50/always`'s frame count. I re-ran the **same** harness three times to check whether it was my change: `652, 945, 954`. It is machine jitter on the heaviest arm, not a harness effect — and it is a concrete argument for the deferred iterations-and-median work, now demonstrated rather than asserted.

## Correctness fixes

**Chromium windows were never found.** `class="chrome"` is wrong for Chromium, whose Hyprland class is `chromium`, and the lookup tests `"chrome" in class` — which is `False` for `"chromium"` (I checked in python3 rather than assuming). On a Chromium-only machine the browser launched fine and the runner reported "no window appeared" until timeout. Class is now derived from the binary actually found.

**Failures exited 0.** `run_one "$b" || true` meant a timeout or a browser that never launched still exited 0, so CI recorded a pass and any wrapper read incomplete results. Now non-zero, with `--keep-going` to try the rest and still fail at the end. A server that fails to start exits 1 too, instead of launching browsers against nothing.

**It killed arbitrary processes.** The old lookup was `ss -ltnp | grep -oP "${PORT}.*pid=\K[0-9]+"`, which matches the port number *anywhere on the line* — including inside another socket's `pid=` field — and then killed it. It could terminate an unrelated dev server. Now a pidfile identifies this script's own server, its `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is confirmed before signalling, and a port held by anything else is reported rather than cleared. (The old comment claimed the server was left running for reuse; the code killed and restarted it every invocation.)

**Results overwrote each other and starvation warnings never expired.** `runId` now threads through URL → page → filename. Completion is an exact match rather than "any json newer than a stamp", `history/` is keyed by runId so nothing is destroyed, `latest/` keeps the stable path, and the starvation check reads only this run — it used to glob every historical result, so one starved run from days ago re-warned on every future invocation.

**The 60Hz hardcode made starvation detection blind.** This display measures **240.1Hz in Chrome and 58.75Hz in Firefox**. The hardcoded 60 was accidentally right for Firefox and off by 4× for Chrome, putting the 25% floor at 60 frames where it should be 240 — so a Chrome run starved down to 70 frames passed the check, and its per-frame numbers, divided by that collapsed denominator, read as a large win. Exactly the failure the flag exists to catch. Now measured per run and reported as `refreshHz`.

**`--backend=webgl` under `--disable-gpu`.** `scripts/benchmark.ts` accepted it while launching headless with the GPU disabled, so whatever it printed was not a WebGL number. It now refuses, and is relabelled a Canvas2D CI smoke test.

## Deduplication

- **One `_shared/server.ts`** replaces 24 copies — 21 byte-identical, 3 differing only in a default port. Duplicating a server that enforces path containment and cross-origin isolation means a fix has to land 24 times to hold. Ports default to `0` so the OS picks a free one, which is what removed the need to kill anything.
- **One `_shared/build.ts`** replaces 17 near-identical builds (55 lines each, 47 shared, differing in a comment and a `<title>`). The **eight wasm benchmarks keep their own**, because copying a `.wasm` into `page/` is real logic, not boilerplate. `--external` emits a source-mapped `benchmark.js` so a profile attributes frames to `Scene.ts` instead of `(index):1`.
- `_shared/client.ts` holds the refresh calibration and result envelope.

Caught during this: `hero-metrics` imports the `@vectojs/devtools/headless` **subpath**, which my first resolver regex missed. Its build broke, I found it by running all 24, and the shared resolver now handles any `@vectojs/<pkg>/<subpath>`.

## Tooling

`shellcheck` and `shfmt` join the `check` gate, following `actionlint`'s locally-optional/CI-enforced pattern; all four shell scripts pass. `.gitignore` moves to 6 wildcards from 21 per-benchmark rules — the list had fallen behind, and `f32-simd-eval/page/index.html`, a 200KB+ generated bundle, was covered by no rule and would have been committed.

## The headed path is untouched

`hyprctl dispatch exec [workspace N]`, real `/usr/bin/google-chrome-stable` and `/usr/bin/firefox`, fresh disposable profile, focused window, real GPU. Nothing here moves measurement into headless — the headless `debug-page.ts` and `scripts/benchmark.ts` are both explicitly labelled non-quotable.

## Deferred

CDP tracing, Gecko profiler (`MOZ_PROFILER_STARTUP` + PID lifecycle), the unified result schema, and iterations/median/p95/MAD are recorded in `TODO.md` rather than attempted here. The profiler paths need substantial real-run validation to be worth trusting.

## Verification

`just verify` clean across all 11 packages. 24/24 benchmarks build, bundles byte-identical or within 0.02%. Full headed run of both engines end to end after the refactor, results landing under `history/` and `latest/` as intended.

items.title: Fix four measurement bugs in the eval and difficulty analysis
items.body:
Four bugs found while building an oracle-replay harness for the benchmark. Each one silently distorts a measurement rather than causing a visible failure.

## 1. Malformed guesses aborted the sample

`GameState.guess` raises `ValueError` on input that is not a single letter. That propagated out of the tool and errored the entire sample, so the game was **dropped from the results** rather than scored. A model that emits `"ab"` disappeared from the win rate instead of being penalised by it — which biases results upward, and more so for weaker models.

The tool now records the attempt and raises `ToolError`, which is reported back to the model so it can correct itself.

## 2. Repeats and malformed guesses were invisible

`GameState.guess` returns early on a repeated letter, so neither repeats nor rejected input ever reached `guessed_letters`. No analysis built on the store could see them.

`GameState` now records every submission in `attempts`, and the scorer reports `num_repeated_guesses` and `num_invalid_guesses` alongside it.

Feedback shown to the model on a repeat is **deliberately unchanged**, so task difficulty is unaffected and results stay comparable with previous runs.

## 3. `filter_candidates` was over-inclusive

It matched the board with a regex in which `.` also matches the guessed letter, so the board `.a.a.a` admitted `aaaaaa` — an unreachable state, since guessing a letter reveals every occurrence at once. Revealed letters are now matched on position set.

**This changed a solver metric for 72 of the 100 dataset words.** Regenerated reports are included.

It also weakens a result the analysis README relies on. Spearman correlation between the dataset's difficulty labels and computed difficulty:

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wrong_coverage` | +0.119 | **-0.008** |
| `wrong_freq_raw` | +0.198 | **+0.026** |
| `wrong_info_gain` | +0.449 | **+0.368** |

The labels are essentially uncorrelated with computed difficulty, more clearly than the old numbers suggested.

## 4. Difficulty measured against a dictionary missing two of the words

A solver cannot converge on a word its dictionary lacks: the candidate set empties and the run degenerates into guessing the alphabet, inflating that word's difficulty instead of measuring it.

`dwarves` and `pyjamas` are absent from `wordlist.txt` — which is why `dwarves` scored `wrong_coverage` **16 rather than 1**. `measure_difficulty.py` now unions the dataset into the dictionary and reports what was missing.

## Testing

23 new tests across `tests/test_hangman.py`, `tests/test_e2e_hangman.py`, and a new `tests/test_analysis_solvers.py`, covering attempt recording, malformed-guess recovery end to end, and the corrected candidate filter. All pass.

## Notes for review

- **One pre-existing test still fails**, untouched by this PR: `test_hangman_incomplete_game` asserts a message limit of 44, but `_calculate_message_limit` returns 57 since the turn-limit change moved from 3 to 4 messages per guess. The test is stale in three separate ways (the constant, the number of mock outputs needed to reach the limit, and an assertion on the final message role). Fixing it needs a decision about what the test is meant to pin, so I left it as found rather than guessing. It fails identically on `main`.
- Also removes an unused `csv.Sniffer` in `extract_wordlist.py` — the only `ruff` failure under `analysis/`.
- Regenerated data files (`difficulty_report.tsv`, `difficulty_binned*.tsv`, `reclassified_from_*.py`) account for most of the diff size.

items.title: Fix six measurement accuracy bugs
items.body:
Found while auditing the measurement path for accuracy. Each item is independent; happy to split into separate PRs if you prefer.

## 1. `doNotOptimizeAway` falls back to the slow path on clang-cl — fixes #111

The three guards around `doNotOptimizeAway` tested only `_MSC_VER`, but clang-cl and clang in MSVC compatibility mode define `_MSC_VER` **and not** `__GNUC__`:

```
$ clang++ --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -dM -E -x c++ /dev/null | grep -E '__GNUC__|__clang__|_MSC_VER'
#define _MSC_VER 1933
#define __clang__ 1
```

So those builds went through `doNotOptimizeAwaySink(&val)` — a non-inlinable call compiled under `#pragma optimize("", off)`, executed inside the measured loop on every iteration — instead of the inline-asm barrier. That is both slower and a weaker barrier, i.e. it distorts exactly what it is meant to protect. The implementation is now selected by what the compiler understands, the same way google/benchmark does it.

The MSVC-only `#pragma optimize` pair is nested inside its own `defined(_MSC_VER)` check, so a compiler that is neither GNU/clang nor MSVC no longer hits an unknown pragma (that path is compile-tested).

## 2. `epochIterations()` was silently ignored when `warmup()` was set

The warmup epoch fell through to upscaling instead of measuring. With `epochs(5).epochIterations(1000).warmup(100)`:

```
before: iterations per epoch: 381617 373323 1000 1000 1000
after:  iterations per epoch:   1000   1000 1000 1000 1000
```

Besides breaking the documented "run *exactly* these iterations" contract, it mixed epochs of very different sizes into the median.

The rule "an exact iteration count overrides any calculated one" was written in three places; it is now one `calcNextNumIters()` used by every state, which also removes the unguarded `calcBestNumIters()` on the `upscaling_runtime → measuring` transition (unreachable today, but only by a non-obvious invariant).

## 3. `relative` column ignores `batch()` — fixes #131

It compared raw epoch runtimes while every other column in the row is per unit, so the percentage was off by exactly the ratio of the batch sizes. In the new test (equal per-item cost, `batch(100)` vs `batch(200)`) the column read ~51%; it now reads ~102%, consistent with the `ns/item` column next to it. Identical output when the batch sizes match, which is the common case.

## 4. `medianAbsolutePercentError` returns NaN for a zero measurement

`(x - med) / x` is `0 / 0`. The NaN reaches the `err%` column and the CSV/JSON output, and it breaks the strict weak ordering `std::sort` requires inside `calcMedian`. Reachable from any measure that is 0 in some epochs — pagefaults, contextswitches, branchmisses. A zero measurement now yields the limit of `|(x - med) / x|` as `x → 0`: zero when the median is zero too, infinite otherwise.

## 5. Performance counters were not compensated for multiplexing

When more events are monitored than the hardware can count at once, the kernel time-shares them and returns only what happened while an event was scheduled — so `ins/op`, `cyc/op`, `IPC` and the branch columns were silently **too low**: with the NMI watchdog holding a counter, under another running perf tool, or on a VM with a restricted PMU.

`time_enabled`/`time_running` were already being read into members and then never used. They now scale the counters the way `perf stat` does. Note that `PERF_EVENT_IOC_RESET` does *not* reset those two — I verified they accumulate over the event's lifetime — so the scaling uses the difference to the previous read. Scaling happens in `endMeasure()`, at the read point, so `calibrate()`'s overhead data ends up in the same unit as the measurements it is subtracted from.

This is the one change I could not exercise end-to-end: hardware counters are unavailable in the container I worked in. It is a no-op whenever `enabled == running`, which is every non-multiplexed run.

## 6. Undefined behavior in the iteration-count math

`calcBestNumIters` could cast a non-finite or out-of-range double to `uint64_t`: an epoch measuring 0 elapsed time (possible with a coarse clock) makes the division produce infinity, and NaN when the target runtime is 0 as well. `upscale`'s `mNumIters * 10 < mNumIters` overflow check also missed values that wrap to a smaller positive number. Both now go through one `detail::u64(double)`, which also hardens the pre-existing `suggestedIters` cast.

## Testing

- 43/43 test cases pass on gcc 13 and clang 18, and clean under ASan + UBSan.
- Header compiles warning-free under `clang -Weverything` and `gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -Wold-style-cast -Wfloat-equal -Wsign-conversion` for C++11/14/17/20; `clang-format` clean.
- New coverage: `test_warmup_with_exact_iters` (added to `unit_exact_iters_and_epochs.cpp`), `unit_mdape.cpp`, `unit_relative_batch.cpp`.
- Sanity check against ground truth (min of 7 long single runs) is unchanged: reported median lands within ~1%, run-to-run spread ~0.5%.

## Note

`docs/reference.html` still shows the old `relative` formula. I did not regenerate the docs since that produces a large separate diff and you have a dedicated commit for it — the doc comment in the header is updated.

items.title: ✨ feat(benchmarks): end-to-end sparse LM-head benchmark + backbone support decision (#61)
items.body:
Closes both remaining items on #61: the end-to-end benchmark and the LLaDA/MDLM-DiT support decision.

## Benchmark — the step-time win is much bigger than the kernel benchmark showed

`benchmarks/sparse_lm_head_training.py` measures the flag through `DiffusionTrainer.compute_loss` (forward + loss + backward), across the mask-ratio axis #77 identified as decisive. Both arms get the **same pre-noised batch** so they cannot accidentally benchmark different masks, and arms interleave with alternating order so thermal drift does not land on whichever runs second.

RTX 6000 Ada, fp32, B=2 L=512 H=512, 2 layers, 3 trials × 10 steps. Negative = sparse better:

| vocab | mask | step time | d peak | d activ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32000 | 0.15 | **−32.6%** | −25.7% | **−40.9%** |
| 32000 | 0.50 | **−12.6%** | +0.2% | +0.4% |
| 32000 | 0.75 | +1.3% | +21.4% | +34.1% |
| 128256 | 0.15 | **−62.1%** | −22.7% | **−37.4%** |
| 128256 | 0.50 | **−25.7%** | +1.0% | +1.7% |
| 128256 | 0.75 | −4.3% | +27.7% | +45.5% |

`d activ` subtracts the model weights — identical in both arms, so total peak dilutes the effect. Read that column.

**−62% step time at 128K vocab / 15% masking.** That is substantially larger than #77's kernel microbenchmark implied, and the reason is straightforward: end-to-end, the `[B, L, V]` GEMM dominates a small model's step, so skipping most of it matters more than measuring the kernel in isolation showed.

Memory reproduces #77's finding through the real trainer — roughly neutral at the ~50% ratio MDLM training averages (+0.4% / +1.7% activations), clearly worse above it (+34% / +46% at 0.75). **Sparse projection is not automatically a memory optimization**, which is the thing this benchmark exists to state plainly.

**LoRA needs a caveat.** At 128K vocab it is worse than full finetune on memory above ~15% masking (+47.5% activations at 0.50, +112.9% at 0.75), because the frozen backbone's activations already dominate and the `[M, V]` projection plus its autograd graph is close to pure overhead there.

The flag stays **default-off**, but the recommendation is now narrower and more useful than "off": enable for large vocabularies at low mask ratios, where it is a large step-time win at no memory cost. The `sparse_lm_head` field help carries these measured numbers instead of the kernel-only ones.

## Backbone support decision — intentionally unsupported, with concrete reasons

Per the issue's recording rule I inspected current main rather than trusting my earlier notes:

- **LLaDA** — `get_decoder()` *does* return a distinct module (my earlier note was vague on this). But that module emits `logits` at vocab width with no `last_hidden_state`. Routing it through the standard resolver would double-apply the output head.
- **MDLM-DiT** — `get_decoder()` returns **the model itself**, so `_resolve_backbone` yields `None` and there is no separate backbone to run without the head at all.

Both already report unsupported correctly. What was missing was any test proving it: the existing fallback tests use a stub carrying only a `model_type`, so they never touch a real backbone.

Added tests that pin the **causes** rather than the conclusions — if a future LLaDA change starts returning hidden states, or MDLM-DiT starts exposing a separate decoder, those tests fail and prompt revisiting the decision. Plus a defence-in-depth test: `standard_sparse_output` *does* resolve for LLaDA structurally, so only the call-time `TypeError` stands between a mistaken registration and silently corrupted loss and gradients.

**Verification:** 1128 passed, 1 skipped. `ruff check .` clean.


## Two measurement bugs found and fixed during review

**Peak memory included the model weights** (~521 MiB of ~1386 MiB at 128K), identical in both arms, diluting every percentage. `_measure` now also reports activation-only memory.

**`del model, trainer` did not free the model** — they form a reference cycle, so 537 MiB stayed resident until `gc.collect()`. Whichever arm ran second started with the previous arm's weights allocated, which landed in its peak and produced a sign flip between runs. Fixed; all configs re-measured. The activation column was correct throughout (it subtracts the baseline, so the leak cancelled), and both columns now agree in sign everywhere.

items.title: feat: hard timeout + RDFLibReasoner in runtime benchmark, refresh README
items.body:
## Summary
- `examples/runtime_benchmark_results.py` rewritten:
  - **Fixes a real measurement bug**: `StructuralReasoner`'s results were never materialized before timing, so its column measured generator-creation time (near-instant) instead of actual query evaluation -- confirmed ~10x too fast (0.0007s unmaterialized vs 0.0067s materialized on the same query). All reasoner calls now go through `set(reasoner.instances(ce))`.
  - **Adds a hard upper bound** on runtime (`--timeout_seconds`, default 1000s) enforced at the script level via a daemon-thread wrapper. This matters because `StructuralReasoner.instances(timeout=...)` and `RDFLibReasoner.instances(timeout=...)` don't actually enforce anything (confirmed by reading `owlapy/owl_reasoner.py`/`owl_reasoner_rdflib.py` -- only `SyncReasoner`'s does, via real Java-thread cancellation). A reasoner that hasn't returned within the bound is reported as `TIMEOUT(>Ns)` and the script moves on without waiting further.
  - **Adds `RDFLibReasoner`** as a benchmarked reasoner.
  - Removes a `global sync_reasoners` mutation that silently emptied the reasoner list for later `record_runtime()` calls within the same process (discovered while re-running the benchmark for this PR).
  - Keeps the earlier progress logging (`[HH:MM:SS] <reasoner>: i/n done (Xs) -- <class expression>`).
- `README.md`: refreshed the "Reasoners Runtime Benchmark" tables with numbers from the fixed script -- adds the `RDFLibReasoner` column, corrects `StructuralReasoner`'s numbers, marks the cells that hit the timeout explicitly (`TIMEOUT(>1000s)`) instead of showing a misleading elapsed time, and adds a closed-/open-world semantics note linking to `markdown_docs/05_reasoning.md`'s reasoner comparison table.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: documents all of the above under `[Unreleased]`.

## Test plan
- [x] Verified the materialization bug directly: unmaterialized `StructuralReasoner.instances()` call takes 0.0006s vs 0.0067s for `set(...)`-wrapped, same query, same ontology.
- [x] Verified the hard timeout actually triggers and doesn't block: ran with `--timeout_seconds 2` against HermiT on Carcinogenesis, confirmed `TIMEOUT(>2s)` cells and that the script moved on each time rather than hanging.
- [x] `ruff check examples/runtime_benchmark_results.py --line-length=200` -- clean.
- [x] Regenerated both Family and Carcinogenesis tables end-to-end with the fixed script (StructuralReasoner + RDFLibReasoner freshly measured; HermiT/Pellet/Openllet/JFact/ELK/Structural reused from an already-completed full run against the same KGs, since those were already correctly materialized/eager and unaffected by the bug fix).

items.title: docs(#3734): close out — real benchmark pipeline already inlines .push()
items.body:
## Description

#3734 tracked `.push()` on `number[]` compiling to a non-inlined `__vec_elem_set_<N>` helper call in the IR path (10,000 calls in the `array.ts` landing-page benchmark). Its own write-up records that raising Binaryen's inline thresholds "only partially worked" and left the change reverted.

Re-verified directly against the pipeline the real landing-page artifact actually goes through — `compileMulti(..., {})` (no internal optimize) followed by `optimizeBenchmarkWasm()`'s up-to-4-round external `wasm-opt -O4` loop run to a byte-identical fixpoint (`scripts/generate-playground-benchmark-sidebar.mjs` / its `-no-jit` sibling) — rather than a single in-process `compile({ optimize: 4 })` call:

- Zero remaining `call`s to `__vec_elem_set_<N>` inside `bench_array`'s compiled body after the fixpoint (a single-pass `compile({optimize:4})` still leaves exactly one call per iteration — that's the discrepancy, not a naming/measurement bug).
- The optimized binary returns the mathematically correct result (`49995000`), ruling out whole-function constant-folding masquerading as "0 calls".
- Direct timing: ~240µs/call locally — real per-iteration work.

**Conclusion**: the existing repeated-`wasm-opt`-to-fixpoint pipeline (unchanged, already in place) already achieves full inlining. No compiler source change was needed. This PR only updates the issue file with the corrected finding and closes it out (`status: done`). The residual wasm-vs-js gap that remains even with full inlining is a separate, deeper architectural question (WasmGC representation vs. V8 native arrays), not scoped to this issue.

## Test plan

- Docs-only change (issue frontmatter/body). No source files touched.
- Finding independently reproduced via direct `compile()`/`optimizeBinaryAsync()` probes (compile → 4-round external optimize fixpoint → inspect `.wat` call count → instantiate and run for correctness + timing).

Internal/org-member PR — CLA check is skipped automatically.

items.title: fix(test): repair benchmark modules against current APIs, mark them performance (#13162)
items.body:
## Thinking Path

The two modules ran *despite* `-m "not performance"`, which was the first thing to check: neither carried a marker, in either form. So I enumerated every test in both files and asked what it asserts.

**All 24 assert a wall-clock budget or an RSS delta. Not one is functional-only.**

| Module | Tests | Assert elapsed time or RSS |
|---|---|---|
| `performance_benchmarks_test.py` | 10 | 10 (`avg_duration`, `max_duration`, `total_time`, `max_memory_mb`) |
| `system_benchmarks_performance_test.py` | 14 | 14 (`*_time < N ms`, `memory_usage/growth < N MB`) |

That settles classification: both are benchmark suites, both get a module-level `pytest.mark.performance`. In the unit selection a millisecond budget measures the runner's contention, not the code.

Marking alone would have been hiding, though — the tests were red, and a marked-but-broken benchmark is dead weight. So every failure was root-caused and repaired first; the marker only changes *when* they run.

The failures were **API drift, not timing**. 18 tests called signatures that no longer exist, or awaited `MagicMock` doubles standing in for coroutine functions. Two were genuine measurement bugs where the benchmark had drifted onto the wrong subject.

## What Changed

### Shared module — called out prominently

`autobot-backend/conftest.py` stubbed `torch` as a bare `MagicMock()`. `torch.cuda.is_available()` therefore returned a **truthy** `MagicMock`, so any production code guarded by it took the GPU branch and then died formatting `MagicMock` device properties (`TypeError: unsupported format string passed to MagicMock.__format__`). This broke `MultiModalProcessor()` construction for **5 tests across both files**, and would break any future test that builds a GPU-aware object.

The stub now reports no CUDA (`is_available() -> False`, `device_count() -> 0`, `get_device_capability() -> (0, 0)`) — which is the truth on a machine without torch — and registers the same object as the `torch.cuda` sys.modules entry so attribute access and import access agree.

Regression-checked against every test in the repo that touches `torch.cuda` / `gpu_available` / `mixed_precision`, plus all of `multimodal_processor/` and `utils/`: **868 passed, 0 failed** (evidence below).

### `performance_benchmarks_test.py` — 9 fixed

| Test | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `test_llm_response_time_benchmark` | `LLMService.chat` is a coroutine function; patched with `MagicMock` | `AsyncMock` |
| `test_concurrent_llm_requests` | same | `AsyncMock` |
| `test_knowledge_base_search_performance` | `KnowledgeBase.index` (LlamaIndex) no longer exists | mock the successor seam, `knowledge.search.get_vector_search_engine()`; `top_k=5` keeps it on the basic vector path the mock serves |
| `test_knowledge_base_indexing_performance` | `index.insert_documents` gone | mock `store_fact()`, the seam `add_document()` now persists through |
| `test_orchestrator_task_planning_performance` | `classify_request_complexity` / `plan_workflow_steps` are coroutine functions; never awaited — the benchmark was timing *coroutine-object construction* | `await` both; `llm_service.chat` -> `AsyncMock` |
| `test_orchestrator_concurrent_workflows` | same | same |
| `test_memory_storage_performance` | `store_memory(memory_type=…, context=…)` — neither keyword exists | real signature `(category: MemoryCategory, content, metadata)`; context moves into metadata |
| `test_memory_retrieval_performance` | `retrieve_memories(query=…)` — no `query` parameter; selection is by category | store across three categories, benchmark a read of each; assert non-empty |
| `test_end_to_end_workflow_performance` | three `MagicMock` doubles whose returns are awaited | `AsyncMock` |

Also: the memory benchmarks now use a throwaway SQLite file. The default `db_path` is the repo-relative `data/unified_memory.db`, so the fixed tests would otherwise have written 65 benchmark rows into the working tree.

### `system_benchmarks_performance_test.py` — 9 fixed

| Test | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `test_config_service_caching_performance` | `ConfigService.get_all_settings` never existed | `get_full_config()`; see "measurement bugs" below |
| `test_multimodal_processor_performance` | conftest torch stub | shared fix |
| `test_system_startup_performance` | conftest torch stub | shared fix |
| `test_statistics_tracking_performance` | conftest torch stub | shared fix |
| `test_concurrent_processing_performance` | conftest torch stub + measuring the wrong subject | shared fix; see below |
| `test_multimodal_processor_scalability` | conftest torch stub + measuring the wrong subject | shared fix; see below |
| `test_memory_manager_performance` | `MemoryManager.store_task` and `memory_manager.TaskPriority` do not exist | `create_task_record()` (synchronous — the old form spun up and tore down 50 event loops via `asyncio.run` just to call it); `TaskPriority` imported from the `memory` package |
| `test_environment_variable_parsing_performance` | `ConfigManager._parse_env_value` retired | benchmark the canonical `autobot_shared.env_utils` coercions (`env_flag`/`env_int`/`env_float`/`env_str`), one case per type the retired helper covered |
| `test_configuration_file_loading_performance` | `ConfigManager(config_file=…)` — it takes a config *directory* | write the large YAML to `<tmpdir>/config.yaml`, pass `config_dir` |

### Measurement bugs — thresholds untouched

**No threshold in either file was loosened.** Two benchmarks were measuring something other than their stated subject:

1. **`test_concurrent_processing_performance` / `test_multimodal_processor_scalability`.** Once the processor could be constructed, these failed on the clock (611 ms vs 500 ms; 3 940 ms vs 2 000 ms). Profiling isolated it: `MultiModalProcessor.process()` writes every result to the shared SQLite memory database via `_store_result`, and concurrent writers serialize on that file's write lock.

   ```
   full process x10:               235.7 ms
   without _store_result x10:       11.9 ms   <- 95% of the span
   without auto_optimize x10:      408.9 ms   <- not the cause
   ```

   These benchmarks already mock the compute sink ("mock the context processor for consistent timing"); leaving the persistence sink live made them time disk contention rather than the processor's concurrency. Mocking it too completes the fixture. Budgets stay at 500 ms / 2 000 ms.

   `test_concurrent_processing_performance` additionally now **proves** concurrency directly — a peak-in-flight counter asserts all 10 calls were inside the modality processor simultaneously. If `process()` ever serialized, that peak collapses to 1 regardless of how fast the run happened to be. The clock no longer carries the claim alone.

2. **`test_config_service_caching_performance`** asserted `cached_call_time < first_call_time * 0.5` — two sub-millisecond samples raced against each other, so one scheduler hiccup on the second call inverts it under parallel load. Replaced with the property that *defines* a cache: a hit returns the very object it stored, a rebuild returns a fresh dict. The absolute `cached_call_time < 5.0 ms` budget is unchanged.

Note (not a blocker): comma-separated env values have no canonical list helper in `env_utils`; `env_str` is the current behaviour and the benchmark reflects that.

## Verification

Before, on `origin/Dev_new_gui` @ `8b8767a23`, unit selection:

```
$ python3 -m pytest autobot-backend/performance_benchmarks_test.py \
    autobot-backend/system_benchmarks_performance_test.py -q -p no:cacheprovider \
    -m "not integration and not slow and not distributed and not performance"
18 failed, 6 passed in 8.68s
```

After — unit selection, all 24 correctly deselected as benchmarks:

```
collected 24 items / 24 deselected / 0 selected
============================ 24 deselected in 0.24s ============================
```

After — benchmark selection, all 24 green, budgets unchanged:

```
$ python3 -m pytest autobot-backend/performance_benchmarks_test.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -m performance
============================== 10 passed in 4.38s ==============================

$ python3 -m pytest autobot-backend/system_benchmarks_performance_test.py -q -p no:cacheprovider -m performance
============================== 14 passed in 5.22s ==============================
```

Shared-module regression sweep (every test touching `torch.cuda` / `gpu_available` / `mixed_precision`, plus `multimodal_processor/` and `utils/` in full):

```
175 passed in 4.04s                                    (gpu detection, hardware, profiler, eviction, embeddings)
109 passed, 40 warnings in 36.74s                      (api hardware/multimodal/gpu-monitoring, vector engine)
584 passed, 14 skipped, 2 deselected in 348.90s        (multimodal_processor/ + utils/)
2111 skipped in 16.66s                                 (api_endpoint_migrations_test.py)
```

868 passed, 0 failed.

Lint:

```
$ python3 -m isort --settings-path=. --line-length=120 <files>   # clean
$ python3 -m black --line-length=120 <files>                     # 3 files left unchanged
$ python3 -m flake8 --config=.flake8 <files>                     # 0
$ python3 -m bandit -c .bandit <files>                           # No issues identified
```

Closes #13162

items.title: Add AAA-scale benchmark harness for the World<->GPU mirror bridge
items.body:
Closes #211.

## What

`crates/helio-scenedb/benches/world_mirror_scale.rs` — 5 scenarios against a real GPU device, `harness = false` (matches `pass_timing.rs`'s own reasoning: this measures real wall-clock cost of GPU-submitting operations end to end, not a pure-CPU microbenchmark criterion is tuned for): spawn throughput, steady-state churn, isolated reallocation latency, concurrent buffer access, and flush cost vs. dirty fraction. Full numbers and analysis in `benches/WORLD_MIRROR_SCALE_BASELINE.md`.

## A scoping finding before a single number was taken

The issue proposed "N threads calling `world.insert()` concurrently." That scenario doesn't exist to measure — `World::insert(&mut self, ..)` structurally prevents two threads calling it on the same `World` at once (the borrow checker forbids it). Scenario 4 measures what's actually reachable concurrently instead: `SceneGpuStore`'s own `&self` methods, called directly by multiple threads on disjoint rows — the shape a future parallel-mutation API would need. Documented in the bench's own module doc so this doesn't get re-proposed as a gap later.

## A real measurement bug caught during development

The bench fixture's `#[gpu]` fields defaulted to `DirtyTracked` mode, which defers writes — scenarios 1/3/4 never called `flush_gpu_mirror` or checked the right buffer map, so they were silently measuring CPU-only bookkeeping. Caught because scenario 1 reported **zero** reallocations at every scale, including 1,000,000 entities, which is obviously wrong for a buffer starting at capacity 64. Fixed by switching the fixture to `#[gpu(mirror = Once)]`, which exercises the real growable/immediate write path these scenarios are actually about.

## The numbers (full writeup in the committed baseline doc)

- **Churn at scale is expensive**: 100k entities at 10% per-frame churn costs 44ms/frame (2.6x the 60fps budget) on this subsystem alone; 50% churn costs 263ms/frame (15.9x budget).
- **A single reallocation at 100k→200k rows costs 42.7ms** (2.5x the frame budget), landing wherever whichever `insert()` happens to cross the threshold — direct evidence for #212.
- **New finding, not originally scoped in #212**: growable buffers don't check `wgpu::Limits::max_buffer_size` (256 MiB default) before doubling — a 256-byte packed record hits a real `wgpu` validation-error **panic** at 1,048,576 rows in one buffer. I've added this to #212's scope.
- **Concurrent access gets *worse* per-write as thread count increases** (10k rows: 1 thread → 2.4µs/write, 16 threads → 4.3µs/write, on completely disjoint rows) — direct confirmation #213's lock-contention concern is real, not speculative.
- **`flush_gpu_mirror`'s 0%-dirty baseline is real and non-trivial** (38.5µs at 100k rows) and barely grows with dirty fraction (1% and 10% dirty cost about the same) — confirms #214's O(capacity)-scan concern is the actual bottleneck.

## Also fixed: a real portability gap in `#[derive(SceneStore)]`

`helio-scenedb` gains its own `gpu` feature (default-on). The derive's generated `#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]` gate checks the *consuming* crate's own Cargo features (wherever the macro's tokens get spliced in), not `pulsar_scenedb`'s — so any crate other than `pulsar_scenedb` itself using the derive needs a same-named `gpu` feature for the GPU-column methods to compile at all. This bench is the first consumer of the derive outside `pulsar_scenedb`'s own tests, which is how this surfaced.

## A separate, real blocker found and NOT fixed here

Updating `pulsar_scenedb` exposes a pre-existing, latent `Cargo.lock` issue: two incompatible `windows-core` versions (0.58.0 via `gpu-allocator`, 0.62.2 direct in `wgpu-hal` 30.0.0) already coexist in the checked-in lockfile, and re-resolving *anything* — confirmed via clean-cache A/B testing, not specific to this dependency — can flip which one `wgpu-hal`'s own DX12 module resolves against, breaking the Windows DX12 backend build. This PR's committed `Cargo.toml` is unchanged from `main` (still requests the full `dx12`/`vulkan`/`metal`/`gles`/`webgpu` feature set) — the numbers above were captured with `dx12` disabled locally (uncommitted, Vulkan backend) purely as a workaround to get real measurements. Filed as its own tracked issue, not addressed in this PR.

items.title: perf(interp): keep loop-carried locals in registers
items.body:
## Summary

- keep eligible call-free loop-carried scalar locals authoritative in ARM64 registers across native back-edges
- commit carried values on guard exits, fallbacks, safepoint yields, and module completion while preserving them across cache barriers and continuations
- conservatively reject unsupported plans and retry without carried registers under register pressure
- add planner/lowering regression coverage and document the ownership and benchmark results

## Impact

Five-pair interleaved A/B medians on Apple M4 Pro (`darwin/arm64`, Go 1.26.2, `-benchtime=300ms`):

- IterativeFib(30): 91.75 ns -> 36.75 ns (-59.9%)
- TypedArraySum(256): 673.2 ns -> 307.7 ns (-54.3%)
- Sieve(256): 2,645 ns -> 1,626 ns (-38.5%)
- other canonical default medians stayed within 0.9%; allocations unchanged

## Validation

- `make lint`
- `make test`
- `go test -race ./interp -count=1 -timeout=10m`
- targeted loop-carried/JIT ARM64 tests
- `make check-generated`
- `make benchmark-pr`

Closes #163

items.title: perf(linalg): read the Cholesky input through typed storage — Cholesky256 −4.3% (T1090)
items.body:
`cholFactor` read its input with `AtF64` once per element of the column sweep, which walks the shape to a flat offset and dispatches on the storage type every time. It now takes the contiguous F64 slice once; any other dtype or layout keeps the accessor, and the two inner arms are duplicated rather than sharing a helper — this is the inner loop of an O(n³) factorization, and a closure or a per-element branch gives back what the typed read wins (#755).

| | before | after | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Cholesky256` | 1404070 | 1341497 | **−4.3%** |
| `Cholesky512` | 9325396 | 9029840 | **−2.7%** |
| `Factor256` (control) | — | — | +0.9% drift |

Three interleaved arms, minimum of 6 each. Small, and stated as such: a few percent above a control drifting under one.

## The profile said 57%, and it was the fixture

A first reading put `AtF64` at 57% of this benchmark, promising a far larger win. Chasing where the calls came from: **88% of them are in `spd`**, the test helper that builds the SPD input. It is O(n³) with per-element `AtF64`/`SetF64` and runs once per benchmark invocation, so at n=512 it swamped the factorization it exists to feed — and made the accessor look like the factorization's problem.

It now walks storage too. A fixture that dominates the profile of the thing it sets up is a measurement bug, not a style one. This is the second time this session a profile has been read as production cost when it was test scaffolding.

## PS1005 already flagged this line

As with the reflection sort in #747, the check was right and had been for a while; nothing was wrong with detection. The constraint in this program is ranking candidates by whether a benchmark can see them, not finding them.

items.title: Fix up convolution gradient benchmarks and correctness tests
items.body:
Follow-up to #128, fixing a measurement bug in `bench/ConvVjpBench.hs` plus
naming/doc uniformity. Benchmark-only; no library behaviour changes.

## The `S-artifact` fix

`S-artifact` (and the exec-only setup pre-forcing) forced AST/artifact values
with `length . printArtifactSimple`. That **timed pretty-printing, not
building**: the AST has no `NFData` (see `BenchMnistTools`: `-- no NFData for
AST`), so print was the only full-force, and it dwarfed the ~0.5 ms build
(reported up to ~2.8 s). It could also be **CSE-collapsed** — the fixed-input
body is byte-identical to the shared `artifact` binding, so some sizes returned
a cached value (`inp-192` 658 µs vs `inp-96` 2780 ms).

Fix: force to WHNF, as `mnistTrainBench2VTC` does — with `StrictData`, WHNF
fully builds the AST. `S-artifact` is now a stable ~0.5 ms (matching the
`S-fullpipe-honest − S-fullpipe-hoisted` differential), and setup pre-forces via
`evaluate` rather than `length (print …)` (a speedup: all setup runs before
`defaultMain`).

## Uniformity / doc fixups

- Uniform `HandwrittenVectorized` naming for the size-scaled benchmarks
  (functions + all twelve tasty labels), replacing abbreviated `HandwrittenVec`.
- A note on why shrinking/padded gradients take `@2 @2` (`nKh1 = nKh − 1`) vs
  Same's `@3 @3`.
- Completed the `ConvVjpBench` variant list (`H-exec-contracted`/`H-exec-var`).

## Validation

`S-artifact` at 48×48: 23.2 ms → 530 µs, stable across sizes; a back-to-back A/B
leaves the exec variants unchanged within noise; CAFlessTest 670/670.

items.title: benchymark: add the rendering benchmark
items.body:
Adds [benchymark](https://github.com/moWerk/benchymark), a rendering benchmark for AsteroidOS watches, so it can be installed with `opkg` rather than built by hand. Twelve fixed phases, each isolating **one** rendering cost path, with the frame rate shown live on the watch and a machine-readable result written to `~/.local/share/benchymark/last-run.json`. ### Why it might be useful beyond curiosity The phases map onto the per-device Qt/GL workarounds in `/var/lib/environment/compositor/default.env`. The standing test for those is "drop the flag and see if the UI still renders fine", which is hard to compare between watches and hard to repeat. With this you get a pair of numbers instead: | variable | phases that move if it matters | |---|---| | `QT_ENABLE_GLYPH_CACHE_WORKAROUND` | `SCALE` vs `RERASTER` | | `QT_OPENGL_NO_BGRA` | `DRAWCALLS`, `DRAWFONT`, `OVERDRAW` | | `QPA_HWC_FORCE_GLES` | `OVERDRAW`, `CLOUDHEAVY` | | GPU frequency pinning in `underclock` | `CLOUDHEAVY` | `SCALE` and `RERASTER` are the centrepiece: the same picture drawn two ways — a `scale` transform versus animating `font.pixelSize` — so their ratio measures the glyph-cache cost directly rather than by argument. On nemo (480x480) it reads 55 against 21. ### The recipe Pinned to `v0.2` (`63b7d14`), following the pattern of the other app recipes in this layer. Filed under `recipes-devtools/` beside `asteroid-qmltester` and `asteroid-hackwatch`, which is where the other developer-facing apps live. Built and verified against this layer on a Qt6 nemo build, and run end to end on nemo (MSM8926, 480x480) and sawfish (390x390). Note for anyone reproducing the build: fetching from GitHub needed `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` pointed at the host CA bundle, because the buildtools sysroot here carries none. That is a local environment quirk, not something the recipe can fix. --- ## LLM grading This project was built with an LLM. Rather than leave that to inference, it is graded against [LLMGD v0.2](https://github.com/moWerk/asteroid-docking-bay) and the result published here — including the parts that do not flatter it.

| flag | | meaning | |---|:---:|---| | **U** — Understood | ✅ **yes** | the human caught real defects the machine had missed | | **T** — Tested | ✅ **yes** | built, packaged and run on hardware, results fed back | | **R** — Read | ❌ **no** | nobody read the complete source before publication | | **X** — External review | ⬜ **none** | the meta-asteroid-community PR is open, not yet reviewed | **Origin** — machine-designed, with unusually specific human direction. | | O0 | O1 | O2 | O3 | O4 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | | 🟪 0.45 | 🟦 0.38 | 🟩 0.11 | 🟨 0.06 | ⬜ 0.00 | | | machine chose design **and** expression | human specced, machine designed details | human designed, machine expressed | machine edited human material | no LLM | O0 and O1 land close together, and that is the honest picture rather than a tidy one. The internal architecture — the per-phase `Loader` split, counting `frameSwapped`, the `RotationAnimator` sweep, the mesh pipeline, the `sceneReady` gate — was machine-designed from a reported symptom. But a great deal of the *visible* design was named outright by the human, down to "fade it in over 200ms, let it stand for 1200 and fade out in 600", "the upper button anchored to vertical centre with its bottom", and "starts from 06:00 and rotates 1.5 times". A stricter reading of those tips the headline to **O1**. ### Why the assurance is A3 and not higher **A3 is the ceiling this way of working can honestly reach.** When a machine writes most of the code, control is not exercised by reading the diff — it is exercised by catching what the code gets wrong. So `R: no` here is the expected state, not a lapse; A4 would require a breadth-review that did not happen. The **U** evidence is the part worth trusting, because it is costly and it repeatedly went against the machine: - **The human diagnosed a measurement bug the machine had asserted was fine.** *"the shapes look butter smooth 50-60fps. but the fps display claims 20. And additionally, the rotation that was supposed to be smooth, does now chopp and jump frames approximately in the framerate it displays."* That is Qt Quick's render thread versus its GUI thread, spotted from the couch. The counter was measuring its own scheduling. - **The human designed the experiment that falsified the machine's hypothesis.** *"Can you install v0.1 once again on nemo so i can rule out issues with the watch"* — a controlled A/B that proved a frame-rate ceiling was the watch, not the app, after the machine had spent a cycle assuming otherwise. - **The human refused a diagnostic question and named the right move.** *"dont make me answer stupid questions … Can you please fucking grep the shitty blue over the code base"* — the grep found `Application.centerColor` overriding the `.desktop` entry in one line, after the machine had proposed a further round of tests. - **The human corrected the machine with domain knowledge it lacked.** *"nemo keep alive is not actually working. are you sure you used the latest qt6 implementation? i only last week updated the flashlight"*. - **The human reversed his own instruction when shown the cost.** *"revert the 8s, the 5% impact is unintended, thanks for the push back"*; and later *"ignore my sort phases by fps, that was foolish"*. **T** is real but narrower than it sounds, and the limit matters: **benchymark has no automated test suite.** Testing means clean-from-`cleansstate` builds, unpacking the resulting `.ipk` to verify its payload, installing to nemo (MSM8926, 480×480) and sawfish (390×390), and running end to end with results read back. The recipe in this PR was built from its pinned `SRCREV` before the PR was opened — which is how a fetch failure was found. The sibling project (`asteroid-docking-bay`) does carry a 543-test suite with planted-bug validation; this one does not. ### What this grade does not cover - **Two watches, not a fleet.** Every number quoted comes from nemo and sawfish. - **The numbers moved three times during development**, each time because the measurement was wrong rather than because the app got faster. Only results from v0.2 onward are meaningful. - **Self-graded.** This verdict was produced by the author's agent — the same agent that wrote the code. The retrieval log below exists so the search can be audited rather than trusted; an independent re-run is the only thing that removes the conflict.
Retrieval log (what was searched, found, and skipped) **Run:** author-side · first run · grader: Claude Opus 4.6 **Searched:** `~/.claude/projects/-home-mo-Git-asteroid-docking-bay/*.jsonl` (7 transcripts), sibling `/` directories for sub-agent output, and all transcripts grepped for continuation backlinks. **Found — benchymark work lives in exactly one transcript:** | id | size | records | method | |---|---|---|---| | `2adde14e…` | 18.9 MB | 6 747 | stream-filtered (236 user turns extracted; 955 benchymark hits) | **Excluded after search, not assumed:** `b6d31eda…` (43.9 MB), `2bdab08b…` (41.9 MB), `b053e086…` (3.6 MB) share the `aiTitle` *"Set up asteroid-docking-bay project repository"* and contain **zero** benchymark hits. Three stub transcripts (<7 KB) contain none either. UUID scan for continuation backlinks returned only BLE service UUIDs — no session fork. No sub-agent directory exists for the benchymark session. **Lexicons run (the standard set, verbatim, over user turns only):** | lexicon | turns matching | |---|---| | U / correction | 36 / 236 | | R / review | 6 / 236 (none benchymark-scoped) | | code-engagement | 10 / 236 | Also counted: **32 `Request interrupted` markers** — the human stopping the machine mid-action, which is itself a costly-oversight signal. **Not read whole:** the 18.9 MB transcript, per the stream-filter method the rubric prescribes for oversized transcripts. **Coverage: full.**

items.title: Record what #49 leaves behind
items.body:
Follows #124. Updates the handoff and regenerates the backlog mirror now that #49 is closed.

**1.0 is two issues**: #122 (Blazor layout, codeable today) and #48 (docs site, still needs a generator chosen). The table is re-sorted so the one that can be picked up cold is first.

**Two lessons from the benchmark work that generalise beyond it:**

- *Adding a project to the solution can break a build that has nothing to do with it.* The Blazor package's nested `dotnet publish` shared an `obj` directory with the outer solution build — latent since #120, exposed by `bench/` widening the graph. Worth knowing if another UI package ever gains a nested build.
- *A benchmark measures the machine as much as the code.* Three measurement bugs each produced a plausible-looking number, and all three were found by asking why a result was **better** than expected. Suspect the flattering result first.

**And one thing that has not earned its keep yet**, recorded as such: the harness compiles in CI and never runs there, so the published numbers will decay silently. The handoff now says to run it before believing the table.

Documentation only.

items.title: perf: optimize count-only scan iteration
items.body:
## Summary

Optimize count-only unbounded MVCC scans by advancing with the encoded user-key cache and deferring decoded key refresh until the iterator remains positioned after a partial count.

## Changes

- Add a count-only scan advance path that avoids decoded `user_key` refresh on intermediate counted rows.
- Keep public iterator positioning correct after partial `count_entries()` calls.
- Add count-path tests for point tombstones, range tombstones, and expired TTL entries.
- Refresh the CRUD RocksDB/Fjall scan comparison report and `todo.md` baseline with the 2026-08-01 focused rerun.

items.title: Performance architecture: measure, then optimise
items.body: Benchmarks each phase of the pipeline before changing any of it, optimises only what the measurements showed dominated, and warns callers before the exponential phase rather than after. ## Measuring first `benchmarks/profile_phases.py` times truth-table construction, prime generation, chart construction and cover solving separately, across four dimensions that do not cost the same: cases, conditions, sufficient share and remainder share. Each sweep is independently seeded, so `--max-width` cannot silently shift the tables below it. Two phases dominate in two regimes: remainder-heavy problems (the parsimonious case) by prime generation, dense on-sets by the cover search. Truth-table construction barely moves with the case count — 25x the cases costs under 2x the time. The harness also exposed a measurement bug in itself: it was paying for prime generation twice, because `build_chart` regenerated what had just been generated. `build_chart` now accepts pre-computed primes. ## Optimising what dominated Prime generation was the bottleneck, and it was spending its time allocating tuples of optional bits. Representing cubes as `(mask, value)` integer pairs instead makes it **141x faster** at eight conditions (1.4135s to 0.0100s), and 83x end to end (2.9913s to 0.0360s). The algorithm is unchanged — this is a representation change, not a different method. Every exactness, chart, R-parity, property and multi-value test passes unchanged, which is what makes it safe to keep. `Implicant.combine` is no longer called internally as a result. It stays as public API and gains a direct test rather than being quietly deleted. ## Warning before the cliff Exact minimisation is worst-case exponential and no heuristic is substituted when a problem gets hard — a silently approximate answer is worse than a slow one. What is negotiable is being told in advance. Once the primes are known the chart shape is known, so `minimize` now raises `MinimizationComplexityWarning` before entering the exponential phase. The run still completes and the answer is still exact. Disable with `complexity_guard=False`. The trigger is the prime count, not the condition count, with thresholds read off the measurements: 53 primes solve in 0.0024s, 78 in 0.60s. The integration tests lower the threshold rather than building a genuinely explosive chart, since such a chart is by construction slow to solve. ## Documentation The complexity table in the minimisation guide quoted estimates, including ~36s for a ten-condition parsimonious solution. It now quotes benchmark output, and that figure is 0.45s. ## Verification 580 tests pass, 100% coverage, mypy strict and ruff clean, docs build `--strict`. --- ## Summary by cubic Measured each pipeline phase, made prime generation drastically faster, and added an early complexity warning so long runs don’t surprise users. Also avoided double work by letting `build_chart` accept precomputed primes and updated the docs with measured timings. - **New Features** - Early warning: `minimize(..., complexity_guard=True)` emits `MinimizationComplexityWarning` before the exponential cover search when prime counts are high; silence via `warnings.simplefilter` or disable with `complexity_guard=False`. Exported at `setqca` and `setqca.minimize`. - Benchmark harness: `benchmarks/profile_phases.py` measures truth-table, primes, chart, and cover across cases, conditions, sufficient share, and remainders (independently seeded). - Chart API: `build_chart(..., primes=...)` accepts precomputed primes to avoid regenerating them. - **Refactors** - Prime generation now uses `(mask, value)` integer bitmasks instead of tuples, making it 141x faster at 8 conditions (1.41s → 0.010s) and 83x end-to-end (2.99s → 0.036s). Algorithm unchanged; `Implicant.combine` remains public and is directly tested. - Docs updated with benchmark results; 10-condition parsimonious run now measures ~0.45s instead of ~36s. Written for commit c1d21599f911cd3c8f5086d32d5e4290449f7204. Summary will update on new commits.

items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #5 (EG optimizer). Makes the scripts reproducible on other servers and fixes a measurement bug that hid most benchmarks' total wirelength.

## Reproducibility

- Remove hardcoded local dependencies from `scripts/run_eg_sweep.sh`: the `conda.sh` path, the env name `diffrouter`, and a machine-specific Potter path.
- `run_eg_sweep.sh` and `run_all_benchmarks.sh` now use whatever `python` is active, and only activate conda if the caller sets **both** `CONDA_SH` and `CONDA_ENV`. `POTTER` defaults to `third_party/Potter` with a clear error if it isn't built.
- Add `requirements.txt` (torch + numpy core; matplotlib optional; rapidwright / fpga-interchange documented as build-/analysis-only).

## Bug fix

`scripts/total_wirelength.py` aborted a whole design when it hit a PIP outside Potter's wirelength table (clock-distribution tiles `RCLK_RCLK_XIPHY` / `CLK_HDISTR`). Those are clock nets, not signal wirelength — the script now skips them (and reports how many). Previously this crashed on 20 of 28 benchmarks, leaving total WL computable for only 8.

items.title: ci: make public baseline inputs declarative
items.body:
Closes #7282

## What changed

The public benchmark protocol now lives in `benchmarks/public-baseline-config.json`. It owns:

- pinned Node/Bun versions
- quiet-host threshold and duration
- measured run counts and warmups for all five components
- the selected honest-bench workloads

`run_public_baseline.sh` consumes those values, and artifact assembly/freshness validation rejects component metadata, runtime versions, or quiet-host policy that disagrees with the config. The app-pattern runner now records the configured warmup/sample counts it actually passes to hyperfine.

The fingerprint now covers the declarative config plus the honest-bench correctness oracle. Honest-bench kernels and fixture generators remain protected as source inputs. Large runner/checker files are plumbing, so logging, cleanup, error handling, and output-format changes no longer require a two-hour regeneration.

## Reproduction and sabotage

Before this change, adding one comment to `benchmarks/json_polyglot/run.sh` changed the harness digest from `28117b86…` to `d9eec9be…` and made the required checker exit 2.

After the change:

- The same plumbing-only edit leaves digest `513dba8f…` unchanged and the checker exits 0.
- Changing `polyglot.measured_runs` from 11 to 12 makes the checker exit 2.
- Changing an app-pattern kernel makes the checker exit 2.
- The harness set shrinks from 47 files / 318,493 bytes to 2 files / 1,544 bytes; the source set explicitly retains the honest-bench kernels and generators.

The existing artifact was green under the broader fingerprint before this change. An exact old-digest → new-digest migration accepts only this narrowing; any later input edit misses the pinned destination and hard-fails. No measurements or artifact values were changed.

## Validation

- `python3 -m unittest tests.test_public_baseline` — 11 passed
- `python3 benchmarks/ci_public_baseline_check.py`
- Config/plumbing/kernel sabotage in both directions
- `bash -n benchmarks/run_public_baseline.sh benchmarks/app-patterns/run.sh`
- `shellcheck -e SC2162 benchmarks/run_public_baseline.sh benchmarks/app-patterns/run.sh`
- Orchestrator smoke: config parsed and stopped before build on the host's Node-version mismatch

- `python3 -m json.tool benchmarks/public-baseline-config.json`
- `bash scripts/check_file_size.sh`

items.title: benchmarks: measure speed inside real browsers, not just Node
items.body:
## What & why

Phase 2 of #107. The speed suite now also runs inside real browsers — Chromium (V8) and WebKit (JSC, the engine behind Safari and every iOS browser) — because engine differences move our headline ratios materially (the ~2× playground reports from an iPad turned out to be JSC, not a measurement bug). Same benchmarks, same tooling: the harness bundles the *same* candidate registry, the *same* fixtures, and the *same* mitata measurement core into a page; Playwright is only the launcher. Each engine emits an ordinary `suite: speed` document distinguished by `env.runtime`, appended by CI onto the same `speed.yaml` stream — which is exactly what the runtime picker from #113 was built to display.

- **`bench/browser/`**: esbuild bundles candidates + mitata benches; a local server serves fixtures with COOP/COEP (Chromium gets `crossOriginIsolated` and 5µs timers); a playwright-core driver collects results and emits the document. The 10 MB JSON fixture is skipped in-browser (logged, not silent); browser resolution adapts between the local dev cache and CI's standard Playwright install, one code path.
- **CI**: `benchmark.yml` installs Chromium + WebKit and runs both legs after the Node matrix, each under the existing best-effort pattern so a browser failure can't discard Node results. WebKit runs only in CI (no local binary) — its first real numbers arrive with the first post-merge push.
- **Cross-environment bugs found by making the suite browser-capable**: `bench/oracle.ts` decoded `!!binary` via Node-only `Buffer.from` (now portable), and `bench/candidates.ts` used `createRequire` (blocked static bundling; now static JSON imports).
- **Memory provenance follow-up from #113**: the old env-less emitter died with that merge and the interim document is backfilled on `benchmark-data`, so `MemoryDocSchema.env` is now **required** and the memory seed is refreshed to the newest migrated document.

Honest first numbers — Chromium, block-YAML parse, this machine, single local run (timings drift; CI produces the published data):

| workload | js-yaml ÷ lightning-yaml | yaml ÷ lightning-yaml |
|---|---|---|
| small config (~1 KB) | 2.66× | 26.8× |
| medium config (~100 KB) | 2.70× | 26.0× |
| large config (~1 MB) | 3.20× | 24.0× |
| medium nested | 2.26× | 19.9× |

lightning-yaml is the fastest YAML parser on every workload in-browser, with a narrower lead than Node's — real engine truth the site will now publish.

## Correctness gate

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (root + the harness's own DOM-lib config)
- [x] `pnpm test` (consistency vs. the oracle) — 59/59
- [x] `pnpm test:unit` (436/436) and `pnpm test:stringify` (218/218) — oracle/candidates changed
- [ ] `pnpm test:suite` — n/a, no parser changes
- [x] `pnpm bench:self` clean + emitted docs validate; **`pnpm bench:browser chromium` end-to-end (146s), emitted doc validates**; `webkit` errors gracefully without a local binary; `pnpm validate:benchmarks` 4/4 under the required-env schema; `cd site && pnpm build` green

Gate was run twice — before and after rebasing onto #115's `src/core.ts` extraction — including a full re-run of the Chromium leg to prove the browser bundle works against the new barrel layout.

## Changeset

- [x] This PR touches `src/` and includes a changeset (`pnpm changeset`, or
      `pnpm changeset add --empty` if it ships nothing to users), **or** it
      doesn't touch `src/` and needs none.

## Correctness note

Not applicable — no parse/dump behavior change to the shipped library. (`bench/oracle.ts`'s `!!binary` decode moved from `Buffer.from` to `atob` — differential-aid plumbing, byte-identical output, covered by the consistency suite.)

items.body:
## Problem

Cold benchmark runs charged one-time shared backend init (Metal shader
compilation, Core ML ANE compile cache) to whichever model happened to
load first, e.g. `tiny.en` `modelLoadMs = 12,586ms` while the 2x-larger
`base.en` loaded in `69ms` in the same run (warm `tiny.en` = `84ms`).
That makes per-model load numbers misleading and unstable across
machines and first runs.

## Fix

- Add an untimed warm-up pass before the timed per-model benchmark
  loop: load-and-drop a backend context for the smallest selected
  whisper model (whisper models share one Metal init cost), plus one
  entry per selected non-whisper backend family (Core ML, sherpa-onnx
  Parakeet), each of which has its own separate shared init.
- Report the measured duration once as a new `BenchmarkReport.sharedInitMs`
  field instead of folding it into any single model's `modelLoadMs`.
  It's real first-launch latency, just not a per-model attribute.
- Emit a `"priming"` progress step for the warm-up pass so the UI
  progress/step count (`steps_per_model` math) stays truthful.
- Factored the warm-up target selection into a plain, unit-tested
  `warmup_plan()` function (handles: no whisper models selected,
  picking the smallest whisper model among several selected, warming
  each selected non-whisper backend family once).
- Documented (without re-architecting) that `memoryDeltaMb` is a
  sequential-process RSS delta that can be skewed by allocator
  retention from earlier models in the same run — added a doc comment
  on the Rust field, the mirroring TS field, and a UI tooltip.
- Mirrored the new `sharedInitMs` field and `"priming"` phase in the
  frontend `benchmark.ts` types/validator and surfaced it in the
  Performance Lab dashboard header.

## Test evidence (run on macbook via SSH worktree)

```
cd app/src-tauri && cargo check                    # clean
cargo test -- --test-threads=1                      # 371 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
cargo test benchmark:: -- --test-threads=1           # 10 passed (incl. 4 new warmup_plan tests)
```

```
cd app && npm ci && npx tsc --noEmit                 # no errors
npx vitest run src/lib/benchmark.test.ts             # 4 passed
```

Fixes #274

* **New Features**

  * Added a priming phase to benchmark progress tracking.
  * Improved benchmark warm-up handling for more consistent model comparisons.
* **Documentation**
  * Added explanations for shared initialization time and memory increase measurements.
* **Bug Fixes**

items.title: Speed up and refresh simulator sampling benchmarks

labels.name: documentation
labels.description: Improvements or additions to documentation

items.body:
## What changed

- add a reusable `CompiledLossMeasurementSampler` for the atom-loss fixture
- replace per-shot loss trajectories with a self-contained 64-shot CSS frame that masks H/CX/Pauli operations per shot, including CX gates skipped after loss
- vectorize rstim `b8` packing with the shared 64x64 transpose kernel and reuse the worker output buffer
- publish one five-row surface-code table: rstim/Stim precompiled, rstim interpreted/Stim direct, and rstim precompiled with atom loss
- show one-time precompile, Sample, `b8` output, Sample + output, and Samples/s separately; Samples/s uses Sample + output
- exclude stdin/stdout pipe transport from the published total

## Why

The earlier atom-loss path rebuilt work and could fall back to per-shot tableau trajectories. The earlier rstim `b8` writer also packed every output bit through scalar table lookups. Together these made atom-loss sampling and output dominate the comparison.

The new loss sampler compiles the operation plan and noiseless reference once. Its CSS frame carries the ideal circuit and loss masks together, so a CX skipped in only some shots is represented exactly without the previous reference-frame correctness bug.

For output, rstim must transpose its measurement-major bit table into shot-major `b8`; Stim returns an already bit-packed array from `sample(bit_packed=True)`. Therefore Stim's packing work remains in Sample, while its `b8` phase is only byte serialization. `Sample + output` is the fair final-output boundary.

## Recorded result

Surface d=11, r=100; 1,024 shots; 2 warmups; median-total call selected from 7 measured calls on Apple M4:

| Variant | Precompile once | Sample | b8 output | Sample + output | Samples/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| rstim precompiled | 2.925 ms | 4.208 ms | 0.273 ms | 4.481 ms | 228,545 |
| Stim precompiled | 1.115 ms | 16.093 ms | 0.035 ms | 16.128 ms | 63,493 |
| rstim interpreted | — | 7.330 ms | 0.199 ms | 7.529 ms | 136,015 |
| Stim direct | — | 16.775 ms | 0.040 ms | 16.815 ms | 60,896 |
| rstim precompiled + atom loss | 2.979 ms | 4.002 ms | 0.264 ms | 4.266 ms | 240,053 |

In this run, rstim is 3.60x faster than Stim at the precompiled Sample + output boundary. The precompiled atom-loss row is in the same roughly 4.3 ms range as ordinary rstim precompiled; its small lead is treated as run-to-run variation, not an atom-loss speedup claim.

For the atom-loss fixture, one depolarization event and two independent per-atom loss events after every two-qubit gate each use `p = 1 - 0.999^(1/3) = 0.0003334445062`, so the probability of at least one of the three error events remains `0.001`. Depolarization is emitted before loss so the events remain independent under executor semantics.

## Validation

- `cargo test --locked -p rstim --quiet`
- 80 benchmark-runner Python tests
- `python3 tools/check_rstim_vs_stim_compiled_steady_evidence.py --dir benchmarks/rstim_vs_stim_simulator/results/compiled-steady-release`
- portable evidence catalog validation
- site manifest validation
- `make build-site`
- built-site contract validation: 8 checks, 0 warnings, 0 failures
- `git diff --check`

items.title: Year-over-year section change matrix: what changed, how much, and where
items.body:
Benchmark P2 — C2 (YoY section diff) + C3 (deterministic change buckets), in the matrix shape that seeds C4. New Benchmarking view **"YoY Changes"**: rows = taxonomy section concepts, columns = selected peers, cells = how much of that section changed between the filer's two most recent 10-Ks (amendments win their period), heat-shaded by bucket with the exact percentage shown, clicking through to the redline.

## Classification is deterministic and auditable

Symmetric token churn — `(added + removed) / (prior + current)`, capped at 100% — bucketed at **25% major / 10% moderate / 2% minor**, with New/Deleted as their own facts. Measured on the same engine-normalized slices the section-scope filter searches, so "26% of Risk Factors changed" is reproducible from search behaviour. The redline is labelled as normalized text; a section absent from both periods reads `n/a`, never "unchanged".

## Two measurement bugs found during live verification, fixed

1. **diff-match-patch's 1s default timeout** degraded long sections into a coarse everything-changed verdict — a stable section scored **162%**. Word-mode diffing now gets time to finish exactly, and the symmetric ratio cannot exceed 100% regardless.
2. **Running page headers** ("Item 1A" printed atop every page) fragmented sections into page-sized slices — Microsoft's Risk Factors measured as ~880 of ~10,900 tokens and the comparison diffed two *different fragments* (82% artifact). A repeated same-item heading no longer ends its own section. This fix also strengthens B3 section-scoped **search** on every running-header filer.

After both fixes, live AAPL/MSFT matrix reads: Risk Factors 26% major / 16% moderate, MD&A 38% / 33%, Controls 1% unchanged / 9% minor — differentiated and believable.

## Verified

- Live matrix screenshot on AAPL + MSFT with sane per-section numbers; MSFT slice verified at full ~10,200/10,900 tokens post-fix.
- `sectionDiff.test.ts` (7): normalization-invariance, threshold scaling, appeared/vanished, growth symmetry, 100% cap, 12k-token performance. Running-header regression case in `sectionScope.test.ts`.
- vitest 1004/1004, tsc clean, eslint clean.

items.title: Fix mobile navigation performance stalls
items.body:
## What changed

- stop Browse navigation from invalidating expensive source tabs before the destination mounts
- freeze blurred tab trees and cancel/restart deferred Outlook chart staging across focus changes
- defer Search details/index installation until after the first interaction frame
- remove deterministic 30-second audit waits for product-history work that audit mode intentionally suppresses
- attribute responsiveness samples only to time inside each measured phase and yield between synthetic payload benchmark phases
- report product-history cache readiness separately from bank-history readiness

## Root cause

The supplied production trace mixed several issues. Global `activeSection` updates woke mounted off-screen tabs before navigation, Outlook retained and continued heavy staged work across focus changes, and Search installed multi-megabyte optional data on its initial navigation path. The audit also waited for product history on Product/Lender screens even though those screens explicitly suppress that maintenance during an audit, producing two false 30-second failures. Its phase snapshots additionally included timer/frame time that began before the measured phase.

## User impact

Browse and tab transitions avoid cross-screen render fan-out, Outlook no longer remounts all deferred charts on its first refocus commit, and Search can paint before optional details/index work begins. Performance reports no longer classify suppressed history work or pre-phase timing as app stalls.

## Verification

- `cd mobile && npm run ci`
  - Expo Doctor: 18/18
  - script tests: 50 passed
  - Jest: 82 suites / 825 tests passed
  - TypeScript and lint: passed (14 existing warnings, 0 errors)
  - Android, iOS, and web exports: passed
  - artifact size guard: passed

## Summary by Sourcery

Improve mobile navigation and audit responsiveness by deferring heavy work, isolating tab transitions, and tightening performance measurements.

Bug Fixes:
- Prevent Browse tab navigation from waking off-screen tabs and overwriting the active section before the destination screen mounts.
- Avoid deterministic 30-second performance audit failures by not waiting for product-history work that is intentionally suppressed during audits.
- Ensure deferred interaction-based work can be cancelled on blur and still executes if interactions never settle or InteractionManager is unavailable.
- Exclude pre-phase timing from responsiveness metrics so audit lag samples only cover the measured window.

Enhancements:
- Freeze blurred tabs and gate Trends tab history and insights loading on focus to reduce cross-tab work during navigation.
- Preserve deferred Outlook chart staging across focus changes so expensive chart surfaces do not remount from scratch after refocus.
- Defer Search details and index initialization until after the first interaction frame so the initial Search UI can paint before heavy data installs.
- Attribute responsiveness samples to timed intervals and yield between synthetic payload benchmark phases to avoid the audit itself causing stalls.
- Report product-history cache readiness separately from bank-history readiness in the performance audit environment and diagnostics envelope.

Tests:
- Extend navigation, performance audit, interests, observability, and yieldToUi tests to cover new routing, optional-data, interaction deferral, and environment-reporting behaviors.

items.title: feat: compare benchmarks against the last released tag during release
items.body:
Nothing currently stops a release shipping a performance regression. Both benchmark suites measure only the *current* checkout, so a regression is visible only to whoever thought to record the old numbers first — and #17 shipped a deliberate ~34% `clone()` regression that would have gone unnoticed had its author not measured by hand.

`pnpm bench:compare` builds the last released tag and the current checkout, measures both with **this** checkout's harness, and reports the deltas. `/release` runs it as step 4, before the CHANGELOG is written rather than after, because the result belongs in the entry.

## The two halves are not equally trustworthy, and the output says so

**The deterministic half is the gate.** Instantiation counts are identical across runs and machines, so any delta is real. So is the compiled-output check: when `dist/*.js` is identical bar comments, the runtime section is skipped entirely — a stronger claim than any timing run, and how a types-only release avoids reporting noise as a result.

**The runtime half is a smoke alarm.** It alternates the builds across rounds, keeps each row's best observation, and refuses to compare a row whose own repeats disagree. It still resolves large effects only, and the docs say that plainly rather than implying a precision the method lacks.

That wording is not caution for its own sake — it is what testing produced:

| rounds | what it reported for `get()` | truth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **+47.6% regression** | ~4x *faster* |
| 2 | −26.8% | ✓ |

And `clone a built container`, whose true value is ~+34% slower, was reported at `+36.2%` in one run and `−36.8%` in the next — the baseline row measured `0.0265` and `0.0799` on identical code. That is why rows now print `unstable — not compared` when they cannot reproduce themselves, and why the minimum round count is hard-floored at 2. At `BENCH_COMPARE_ROUNDS=4` it lands on `+33.8%`, matching an independent hand measurement.

## Three bugs found by running it rather than reasoning about it

- **Left the repo on a detached HEAD.** Overlay cleanup used `git checkout <ref> -- <path>`, which stages the path; unstaging one absent from the baseline left it untracked, which then blocked the checkout back. Cleanup now owns its copies outright.
- **Cleanup tracked paths at directory granularity.** `src/__tests__/__helpers__` exists at the baseline while `syntheticGraph.ts` inside it does not, so "the directory already existed" left the added file behind.
- **The fast path hashed compiled test output.** `tsc` also emits `dist/__tests__/**`, so any test-only change looked like a runtime change and defeated the skip entirely. Now `-maxdepth 1`, matching what `package.json#files` publishes.

## Why refs switch in place rather than in a worktree

`bench-types.mjs` writes fixtures under `node_modules/.types-bench` that import `../../src`. A worktree symlinks `node_modules` back to the primary checkout, so those fixtures resolve to the *primary* `src/` and report the current commit's numbers under the old tag's name. Documented in the skill's gotchas, since it is the obvious approach and it fails silently.

The script requires a clean tree, refuses rather than stashing on your behalf, and restores the original branch on the way out including when a measurement throws.

## Checks

`pnpm build`, `pnpm test` (9 files / 61 tests) and `pnpm lint` pass. No `src/` changes — this is tooling and documentation only, so nothing here affects the published package.
