items.title: docs(benchmarks): regenerate all reports from the current engine, scrub private paths
items.body:
## Summary

All benchmark reports are regenerated with the current engine so every table in the repo shows the same reproducible numbers, the two benchmark generators no longer overwrite each other's files, and private local paths are scrubbed from all committed artifacts.

## Problem

The repo carried three conflicting benchmark tables for the same four tasks: `docs/benchmarks/README.md`, `docs/benchmarks/dataset-report.md`, and `redcon-benchmarks/README.md` each reported different reductions. Root cause: `run_benchmarks.py` and `build_agent_run_dataset.py` both wrote per-task `.json/.md` files into `docs/benchmarks/` and silently clobbered each other, and two of the documents were stale runs from March. On top of that, 81 committed strings leaked a private local path, and the headline table quoted warm-cache savings (-99%) that `ROADMAP.md` itself flags as a P0 measurement bug.

## Approach

- `build_agent_run_dataset.py` now defaults its output to `docs/benchmarks/agent-run/`, so the two pipelines own separate directories and cannot overwrite each other again.
- All three pipelines were re-run with the current engine: strategy benchmark (avg 79%), agent-run dataset (avg 77.6%), context dataset (avg 82.1%). Re-runs are deterministic (verified by running twice).
- `docs/benchmarks/README.md` (generated) gains a Related Reports section explaining that per-task numbers differ across pipelines by methodology, not staleness.
- `redcon-benchmarks/README.md` is rewritten around the fresh agent-run numbers. Warm-cache figures are withdrawn with an explicit note pointing at the ROADMAP P0 cached-summary bug; the cost model is recomputed from cold-run savings only.
- `redcon-benchmarks/tasks/` is removed; per-task raw data lives in exactly one place (`docs/benchmarks/agent-run/`).

items.body:
## Intent

Fix a benchmark measurement bug: the `generic` column counted internal plan candidate titles, which structurally end in "smoke flow", so the metric could never improve no matter how good user-facing names became.

- Corrected readings on the four pinned targets show the naming work landed: user-facing generic titles are now 0/1/1/0, and the remaining ones are legitimately styled API-checklist flows.

items.title: perf(interp): fold loop branch legs into native back-edges
items.body:
Record native loop fallback exits as branches so loop anchors recompile
through the side-exit machinery, fold partial legs whose cut lands on the
plan's own header into the committing-flush native back-edge, and share
identical scheduled continuations so folded legs that cycle through a loop
nest converge instead of exhausting the continuation limit. Handle the
trapNone return a folded RETURN or completed leg produces in the loop
wrapper: tear the frame down like call() for a function loop and mark the
module frame exhausted like start() for top-level code.

Sieve(256) drops from 4.19us to 1.61us (default) and 4.17us to 1.57us
(eager jit) on M4 Pro interleaved A/B; scan-loop native entries fall from
~55 to ~1 per run. All other benchmarks stay at parity.

Closes #155

items.title: P6.1 Total-pipeline deadline and honest latency measurement
items.body:
Closes #17

## The structural gap

D16 gave `eyes` and `brain` per-role ceilings (30s / 45s) enforced **per attempt inside `client.complete`**. Nothing bounded the whole graph run — the ceilings cap each model call, not their sum plus research and TTS. The tail was unbounded.

## What ships

- **A total-pipeline deadline** via `config["configurable"]["deadline"]` (absolute `time.monotonic()`), checked at each node's entry. No 8th state key — the schema stays at exactly 7. Absence of the key means unbounded, so every existing caller is unchanged.
- **A blown deadline is a degraded success, not an error.** Nodes skip their model call and synthesize from what is already known. `tts_node` is deliberately never gated — skipping it would turn "degraded but spoken" into silence, the exact failure this issue exists to prevent.
- `scraper_data` cap is now configurable.
- `scripts/benchmark_pipeline.py` — n≥5 enforced, median/min/max reported, accuracy scored with the production verifier.
- 443 tests.

## Measurement — and a correction to my own earlier claims

Live sweep, 5 runs per configuration, research path end to end:

| Scraper cap | Median | Verified | Deadline hit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 30.6s | 5/5 | 0/5 |
| 1000 | 20.9s | 5/5 | 1/5 |
| 4000 | 23.7s | 5/5 | 0/5 |

**Two things I reported earlier were wrong:**

1. **The 99.0s round trip was an outlier**, not typical. Median is 21–31s. Every run produced verified-correct output.
2. **"4000 chars of context costs 82.6s vs 7.6s without" was a single-sample queue spike, not causation.** Across 15 runs the cap has no reliable latency effect — min/max spans 19–60s at every setting. The cap stays at 1000 for prompt-size and token economy on a rate-limited free tier, and the code comment now says exactly that rather than claiming a speed benefit it does not have.

The deadline still earns its place — just for bounding the **tail** rather than fixing a typical case. Observed max was 60.3s and the 60s default fired on 1 of 15 runs, degrading gracefully. That trade-off is stated in the code: a user who cannot see a spinner is better served by degraded speech at 60s than full quality at 75s+.

## A measurement bug in the harness itself

Per-stage timings were attributed to the wrong node. `_record` stamps at node **entry**, so differencing timestamps charged each node's wait to the node *after* it — `vision` read as `0.0s` while its time was billed to `research`, and TTS's own duration was never measured. Fixed so duration(i) = t(i+1) − t(i), with the last node closed out against the run's end.

Mutation-proved with a synthetic trace: correct attribution yields `1,3,6,2`; the old code yields `0,1,3,6`.

## Note

This is the **third** time in this project that a measurement, not the product, was the thing at fault — after D17 (a benchmark probe misjudging spelled-out amounts) and D18 (the injection eval's scoring). Each instrument looked authoritative and was wrong. That is why this harness enforces n≥5 and scores with production logic.

items.title: feat(skill): speech-to-text — local, free, model chosen by measurement + the Vokes spoken transcript
items.body:
You said Whisper was just a baseline and HF is where you check — so I checked instead of defaulting.

## Benchmarked both on your actual audio (39-min talk, Apple Silicon, both local + free)

| | whisper-large-v3-turbo | **parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2** |
|---|---|---|
| wall clock | **61 s** | 114 s |
| chars / segments | 34,710 / 1,583 | 35,055 / 312 |
| **"Prolog" correct** | **0 / 9** | **8 / 9** |

**Whisper was faster; parakeet was more correct.** Whisper wrote "Prologue" *every single time* the speaker said **Prolog** — in a talk whose central section is a Prolog technique. For technical content, proper-noun accuracy beats WER and beats speed.

Two things worth recording:

- The Open ASR Leaderboard reports parakeet as the **faster** model. On this machine and this file **the speed ranking inverted.** Leaderboard RTFx is batched throughput on other hardware, so the skill says benchmark your own audio.
- **A measurement bug I made and corrected:** grepping `prolog` also matches `prologue`, which scored the wrong transcript as *correct* and briefly inverted the result. The skill names that trap — it's the could-not-fail shape applied to transcription.

## Ships

- `.claude/skills/speech-to-text/SKILL.md` — setup, model-selection table, and five "report what you could not hear" guards
- The Vokes **spoken** transcript, companion to today's slide capture (#9945)

Terms on the slides but never said aloud — "Gordon Bell", "Tridgell" — are **absent** from the transcript, correctly. A transcript isn't a capture of a talk; the skill says to pair both.

## Connects to your C# stack

`AlephZ-ai/blazor-samples` `ISpeechRecognizer` is a **Kleisli arrow** (`IAsyncEnumerable<byte> → IAsyncEnumerable<Result>`), so it composes with `IAudioConverter` by plain function composition — but it's one-directional and can't be interrupted. The duplex half already exists here: `DebouncedOracle.fs` (echolocation, enforced `L > 0`) and the four-corner closure in `ReceiptScheduler.fs`.

items.title: Settle Phase 2's viewer question with measurements on real GPU hardware
items.body:
- [ ] fix #(issue number) — no issue; this closes the two open Phase 2
  checkboxes in `docs/migration-plan.md`.

- [x] description of feature/fix

  Phase 2 has carried an open question since it was written: whether to
  replace napari with `ndv` or a custom VisPy canvas, deferred until the
  benchmark could run somewhere with a real GPU. It has now run on an M2
  Pro (Metal-backed OpenGL). **The answer is keep napari**, and getting
  there turned up a measurement bug, a statistic being read the wrong
  way, and one finding that is about our own scheduling rather than the
  viewer.

  **The benchmark was dividing by the wrong thing.** It compared display
  cost against the *simulator's* acquire time, which is not what gates a
  live view. On the first hardware-accelerated run that produced
  "display dominates … the empirical argument for ndv" off a 2.05×
  ratio — from a simulator making a 512² frame in 5.4 ms where a real
  1 µs-dwell scan takes 262 ms. Against beam time, display is 4.2% of a
  frame. `_verdict()` now divides by the scan's physical duration and
  reports the sustainable frame rate separately, as the ceiling a
  camera-rate source actually faces.

  **A size sweep settles `ndv` by confirming its diagnosis and inverting
  its conclusion.** Display cost is flat across a 16× range of pixels —
  12.2 / 11.2 / 11.4 ms at 512² / 1024² / 2048², a spread smaller than
  the spread within any single run. At 2048² a float64 frame is 33.5 MB
  and repaints in the time 2 MB does, which rules out upload and draw:
  this is napari's fixed CPU-side per-update overhead, exactly what
  `ndv` exists to remove. But a *fixed* cost is amortised precisely
  where it would hurt, since every real workload's frame time scales
  with data and this does not. Acquire overtakes display between 512²
  and 1024²; against beam time it is 4.7% of a 512² frame and 0.27% of a
  2048² one. The one regime where 11 ms would bite — small frames at
  high rate — is already routed to LiberTEM-live.

  **The load sweep says the remaining risk is ours, not the viewer's.**
  `--load N` runs N CPU-saturating numpy workers during the display
  measurement; `--source camera` times the camera path directly. On the
  M2 Pro, camera source, 512²:

  | load | acquire median | display median | display p95 | display max |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 0 | 5.5 ms | 5.6 ms | 7.6 ms | 516 ms |
  | 4 | 5.6 ms | 3.1 ms | 23.0 ms | 649 ms |
  | 8 | 5.7 ms | 17.8 ms | 23.7 ms | **4031 ms** |

  Acquire is unmoved (3% across zero to eight workers) because a grab is
  IPC and a shared-memory read rather than computation — the process
  split doing its job. Display degrades in the tail a full load level
  before the median, and the median briefly *improves* on the way (load
  holds the CPU in a high-performance state an idle machine drops out
  of). That makes the script's median-derived frame rate misleading
  exactly where a user first notices trouble: 318 fps at `--load 4`
  reads as better than 178 fps idle while p95 tripled. At eight workers
  the worst update is 4031 ms — the GUI thread descheduled outright,
  which no per-update efficiency addresses. `ndv` would shave the 5.6
  ms, not the 4 seconds.

  So the actionable conclusion is a scheduling constraint: whatever runs
  analysis must leave cores for the GUI thread. `viewer/jobs.py` already
  runs one job at a time, so our own fan-out is fine — it is the
  numpy/BLAS and LiberTEM executor threads *inside* that job, which
  default to every core.

  **Camera live views measured at half the scan path** (5.6 ms against
  11–12 ms), which is what the `autocontrast_every_frame=True`/`False`
  split in `viewer/live.py` predicted but nobody had checked. The scan
  figures above are therefore the pessimistic half of the pair.

  Also in here: `uv.lock` regenerated for the `camera` extra, which
  landed in `pyproject.toml` without the lock being refreshed.

- [ ] tests added/passed — **no new tests.** This is a benchmark script
  and the documentation of its results; the script is not part of the
  package and is not run in CI. The existing suite is untouched and the
  only source change outside `scripts/` is `uv.lock`.

- [x] add an entry to the changelog — two, under Fixed.

items.title: bench: tile the decode vocab head so tok/s measures on every ANE family
items.body:
Fixes the root cause behind the `n/a` decode column in [`ROOFLINES.md`](bench/results/ROOFLINES.md) (only M5 reported a decode number; M1/M1 Max/M2 were all `n/a`).

## Root cause
`bench/decode_measurement.py` built the vocab head as a single untiled matmul `h @ Wvocab.T -> [B, 32000]`. 32000 exceeds the **16384 max matmul dimension on the A13-A15 families** (M1 = A14, M2 = A15), so the ANE decode row raised `NotImplementedError: ... exceeds ANE family ...'s max dimension 16384; tile the graph or target a higher chip`. Only A16 (M5, max-dim 65536) fit it untiled. The aggregator then correctly reported `n/a` -- it was the benchmark that could not exercise ANE decode on older families, not a measurement bug.

## Change
- **Tile the vocab head** along the output axis so no matmul output dim exceeds `LMHEAD_TILE = 16384` (32000 -> chunks of 16384 + 15616). Tiled the *same way on every chip* (fixed size, not gated on the family cap) so the number stays comparable across generations.
- **Reframe `ROOFLINES.md`**: `Peak fp16 GEMM (TF/s)` is now called out as the headline compute metric (measured on every machine), and the decode column is footnoted as migrating (#181) until the landed machines re-run.

## Verification (Apple M5 Pro)
Tiled vs untiled ANE output is **bit-identical** -- the tiling only splits the matmul, it changes nothing numerically:
```
tiled vs untiled (ANE)  max|delta| = 0.00e+00   relerr = 0.00e+00
tiled vs numpy          relerr = 1.17e-02   (same as untiled; fp16 baseline)
chunks = [16384, 15616]  max_chunk <= 16384
```
- `ruff check` clean on both files; `py_compile` OK.
- `python3 bench/aggregate_rooflines.py --check` passes (ROOFLINES.md regenerated in this PR).

## Notes
- The `roofline_analysis.py` `KeyError: 'ane'` seen in the older JSONs is **already fixed** by #147; those datapoints are just stale (generated at `263e02ff`, before the guard). A re-run picks up the fix.
- Does not close #181: the committed datapoints predate the tiled head, so #181 tracks re-running M1 / M1 Max / M2 (and M5, for an apples-to-apples tiled number) to populate the decode column.

Toward #181.

items.title: Improve reader robustness and lookup performance
items.body:
## Summary

- reject impossible or malformed large containers before destination allocation
- keep memory-mapped readers alive during lookup, decode, and iteration, and release decoder references on close
- reject invalid addresses, invalid UTF-8 during verification, and invalid pointer chains consistently
- reduce reader opening memory and add `DisableStringCache`
- optimize 28-bit tree traversal, recurring string-cache collisions, and reflected struct field lookup
- correct cold-cache and concurrent lookup benchmarks

## Performance

Benchmarks used Go 1.26.4 on Linux/amd64 with `GOMAXPROCS=1` and alternating before/after samples.

- `OpenBytes`: approximately 42% faster and 49.7% fewer allocated bytes
- IPv4 lookup for 28-bit trees: approximately 4% faster
- IPv6 lookup for 28-bit trees: approximately 6% faster
- checked city lookup plus decode: approximately 13% faster
- checked city allocation: 16 B/op and 1 allocation to 0 B/op and 0 allocations
- reused 1,024-entry slice decoding: approximately 16% faster and allocation-free

No allocation regressions were found. Tests against real 24-bit and 32-bit databases in `/var/lib/GeoIP` did not identify a justified traversal rewrite for those formats.

## Validation

- `go test ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- repository commit hooks and linters
- `FuzzDecode` short fuzz run
- focused alternating lookup, decode, container, cache, and concurrency benchmarks

  * Stricter rejection of malformed containers/pointers (including “pointer to pointer”), invalid IP addresses, and invalid UTF-8 in both metadata and decoded data.

items.title: fix(bench): exclude build/infra-failed benchmarks from the XBOW detection solve-rate
items.body:
## Measurement bug (observed live)

XBEN-082's build failed on a **transient `nginx:alpine` TLS-handshake timeout** (docker-hub flake), and the scoreboard counted it as `command_injection 0/1 = 0.0%`. A benchmark that can't be built/started means **the agent never assessed the app** — it's an infra failure, not a detection miss. On a full 104-suite run, every build-rot / registry blip lands in the solve-rate as a miss, **understating** true detection performance.

## Fix — §14 bench honesty (reported, not hidden)

- `XBOWResult.Errored` + `XBOWScoreboard.Errored`. `runOneXBOW`'s no-compose / flag-gen / **build** / **up** / no-target paths (all *before* the agent runs) now mark `Errored`.
- `AggregateXBOW` **excludes** errored results from every detection denominator (overall, by-level, by-tag) and counts them separately.
- `RenderXBOWScoreboard` prints an `EXCLUDED:` line so the failures stay visible.
- `--resume` **re-runs** errored benchmarks (transient infra) instead of carrying them forward + skipping them — a first-pass network blip no longer permanently drops a benchmark.

## Test

`xbow_errored_test.go`: `{solved, real-miss, errored}` → `Total=2`, `SolveRate=0.5` (not 1/3), the errored benchmark's tag/level don't leak into the cuts, and the render reports the exclusion. Non-overfit — no SUT-specific strings; it's infra-vs-detection classification.

items.title: Guard against benchmarking uncompiled Cython extensions + correct the numbers
items.body:
## The bug (measurement, not code)

`hatch_build.CYTHON_TARGETS` cythonizes both `poe_fk` and `refinement` (#248). A dev checkout that built only `poe_fk.so` ran the **refinement** layer (`kinbody_jacobian`, `lm_refine_batch`) in pure-Python mode. The annotated `.py` sources import fine that way, so every functional test passed — but `regen_bench` measured refinement-heavy arms far slower than they ship, and those numbers were committed as authoritative:

| arm | committed (uncompiled) | compiled | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| gen3 | 51.25 ms | **40.75** | −20% |
| piper | 2.50 | **2.01** | −20% |
| xarm7 | 8.87 | **6.87** | −23% |

Only SRS/`_polished`/RR arms move — non-refining arms are within ±7% (machine noise), which is the tell.

## Three guards — bulletproof, single-sourced from `CYTHON_TARGETS`

1. **`regen_bench` gate** — refuses to measure ssik timing unless every perf-target module's `__file__` is a compiled `.so`/`.pyd`. Targets are parsed out of `hatch_build.py` via AST (no `hatchling` import). `--allow-uncompiled` escapes for FK/branch-only refreshes (with a loud warning).
2. **Wheel smoke check** — the cibuildwheel `test-command` asserts each target loads compiled in the *built wheel*, so a wheel that silently failed to cythonize can't publish.
3. **Drift test** (`tests/test_perf_extensions.py`) — pins the gate logic and **fails if a new `CYTHON_TARGETS` entry lacks a matching wheel smoke assertion**, so the guards can't silently fall out of sync.

## Numbers corrected

Re-benched the roster with compiled refinement (per-arm min of two runs). gen3/piper/xarm7 drop ~20%; everything else unchanged (confirming the machine is comparable).

## Test plan
- New guard tests: 3 passed (gate fires on uncompiled, passes compiled, wheel-smoke covers every target)
- Doc-drift + manifest: 102 passed
- Full suite: **1733 passed**, 0 failures
- Verified the gate: fires `SystemExit` on uncompiled, warns+proceeds with `--allow-uncompiled`

Note: this also reframes gen3 — its "51ms" was ~20% dev-measurement inflation; real is ~41ms (still slow vs iiwa14's 5ms, addressed separately by the rescue/batching levers).

##### Performance — 6.1x large-payload speedup

On a 24kb large payload this walked tens of KB per string. Now bounded to `data[:firstQuote]` (the string body only). **128µs → 22µs (5.8x).**
- **SWAR string scan** — replaced two separate `bytes.IndexByte` calls (quote + backslash) with a single inline 8-byte SWAR (SIMD-Within-A-Register) loop that checks for both characters simultaneously. **22µs → 21µs (additional 8%).**
- **Benchmark suite updated** — all comparison libraries (gabs, easyjson, ffjson, etc.) updated to latest versions. Benchmark methodology documented (Apple M4 Max, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs). The `encoding/json` benchmark no longer uses ffjson-generated methods (the [#​126](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/126) ffjson measurement bug was fixed in v1.3.1).
- **README benchmarks refreshed** — all numbers now reflect real measurements on modern hardware with current library versions.

items.title: bench: keep the Track A/B measurement records in-repo
items.body:
`benchmarks/README.md` on master already cites `bge-m3 LongMemEval 81.17 → 48.98`
without the underlying data being present. These are the runs behind that number.

## What this is

107 files, 1.6 MB, under `benchmarks/measurements/`:

- **Track A** — LMEB via mteb for `jina-embeddings-v5-text-nano` (24 files)
- **Track B** — three-model comparison at 23 tasks each: minilm / bge-m3 / jina-v5-nano
- **Two rejected sets**, kept on purpose

They existed only as untracked output in a second working clone of this repo,
which has since been deleted. Until this push they were a single copy on one
machine.

## Why the rejected sets are here

`.CLAMPED-depth100` and `.INVALID-v2439-window` record the shape of two
measurement bugs. The shape is the point: the depth-100 clamp costs LongMemEval
32 points while EPBench moves 0.04, so reading only EPBench would have hidden it
entirely. That distinction — "the model got worse" versus "the harness stopped
measuring the tail" — is not recoverable once the artifact is deleted, and the
builds that produced them no longer exist.

Because they are wrong on purpose, they must not read as results. Every affected
file carries the warning next to the number:

```json
"mean_ndcg_at_10": 48.98,
"invalid": true,
"invalid_reason": "do_recall clamped to 100 in-library on v2.4.38..v2.4.40, ...",
"superseded_by": "trackb_results_v2440_bgem3"
```

A directory-name suffix does not survive a file being copied, and
`jq .mean_ndcg_at_10 **/LongMemEval.json` otherwise returns 81.17, 48.98 and
38.72 with nothing to tell them apart.

## Verification

- No measured value was modified: all 948 pre-existing keys are byte-identical
  to the parent commit; the only added keys are the three above.
- Not shipped to users: `benchmarks/` is absent from both build targets, checked
  against the actual artifacts rather than the config — 0 matching entries in
  `cpersona-2.5.0b1.tar.gz` and in the wheel. This affects clone size only.
- Logs had absolute home paths replaced with `~`; measurements and timings are
  unmodified, and `measurements/README.md` says so.

## Known weakness, recorded rather than fixed

Track B result files do not identify the build that produced them — that lives
in the directory name and in `measurements/README.md`, not in the data. Track A
files do, because mteb stamps `mteb_version` and `dataset_revision`. Emitting
provenance from the Track B harness is follow-up work, not part of this PR.

items.body:
## Why DeerFlow's checkpointer supports two channel modes for the messages channel: full (every checkpoint stores the whole message list — serde and storage grow O(N²) in turns) and delta (LangGraph DeltaChannel: sentinel blobs + per-step writes — O(N)). A storage-layer microbenchmark already proved the algorithmic win, but two production decisions are blocked on evidence it cannot produce: - The snapshot_frequency default. It is currently hardcoded to 1000. Delta mode's read-side cost is a checkpoint-ancestry walk on every graph rehydration, proportional to the distance to the last snapshot — a user-visible latency on state/history endpoints that only appears on the real async saver + Gateway path. - The accessor-graph cache default (_STATE_ACCESSOR_GRAPH_CACHE_MAX = 64): whether it matters depends on how much of a cold state read is graph compilation vs checkpoint reads. This PR builds the production-shaped benchmark that maps the storage-layer gains onto user-visible run, state, and history latency — and includes the first measured matrix. The data says the hardcoded default is untenable; setting the replacement is a follow-up PR. It also fixes a latent correctness gap found along the way: the state-schema adaptation cache was not keyed by snapshot frequency, and DeerFlowClient froze the checkpoint mode but not the frequency. ## What changed - New setting: database.checkpoint_delta_snapshot_frequency (default 1000, same as the previous hardcoded value — no behavior change unless explicitly configured). Like checkpoint_channel_mode, it is process-frozen at first agent build and restart-required; all processes sharing one checkpoint database must use the same value. - DeerFlowClient now freezes the frequency just like make_lead_agent does — embedded (TUI/programmatic) runs can no longer silently diverge from Gateway runs, and the schema-adaptation cache is keyed by the resolved frequency. - New benchmark (dev tooling, not shipped runtime): backend/scripts/benchmark/checkpoint/bench_production.py runs paired full/delta cases in fresh child processes — N turns through the real lead-agent graph with a scripted deterministic model and a real AsyncSqliteSaver, then measures GET /threads/{id}/state and POST /threads/{id}/history through the real Gateway route stack, split into cold/warm accessor-cache samples. Guardrails: cross-mode digest gates void both rows of a pair if materialized state or wire responses diverge; cold/warm cache integrity is asserted structurally (cold must build the accessor graph exactly once, warm must not rebuild); per-turn checkpoint-write cost is measured as merged busy time over LangGraph's concurrent write tasks (a naive latency sum double-counts sqlite queueing and can exceed the turn wall clock), with a write ≤ run invariant in tests. summarize_production.py reports delta/full ratios plus decision metrics (snapshot_write_spike, cache_effect_ms, checkpoint-write share, per-limit history ratios). - Benchmark folder reorganization: scripts/benchmark/ is now grouped per family — checkpoint/ (channel microbenchmark + new production benchmark + shared checkpoint_bench_common.py) and sandbox/. The existing microbenchmark is behavior-frozen: its JSONL schema and its test pin are unchanged. - Docs: AGENTS.md checkpoint sections updated for the knob, the new benchmark, and measured operational limits. ## Surface area - [ ] **Frontend UI** — page / component / setting / interaction under `frontend/` - [ ] **Backend API** — endpoint / SSE event / request-response shape under `backend/app` - [x] **Agents / LangGraph** — agent node, graph wiring, `langgraph.json`, or prompt change - [ ] **Sandbox** — `docker/` or sandboxed execution - [ ] **Skills** — change under `skills/` - [ ] **Dependencies** — new/upgraded entry in `backend/pyproject.toml` or `frontend/package.json` (say what it buys us) - [ ] **Default behavior change** — changes existing behavior without the user opting in (default model, default setting, data shape) - [ ] **Docs / tests / CI only** — no runtime behavior change ## Validation - cd backend && make lint && make test — 9444 passed, 0 failed, ruff clean. - Correctness gates: full vs delta produce byte-identical seed/state/history digests at turns=500 (message_count 1001), cross-process, no middleware threshold tuning. All ratio rows below come from digest-verified pairs; the only failed rows in any run were timeouts, never mismatches.

Measured results (this PR's benchmark, 3 repetitions, medians, payload 128 B, AsyncSqliteSaver on real disk; ratio = delta/full)

turns snapshot_frequency run turn checkpoint write DB bytes state cold history limit=10 history limit=100
500 10 0.50× 0.45× 0.097× 1.03× 1.11× 2.37×
100 10 0.84× 0.80× 0.20× 1.09× 1.23× 2.00×
100 100 1.05× 0.85× 0.18× 1.06× 1.24× 17.4×
100 1000 (current default) 1.80× 0.90× 0.18× 5.79× 74.0× 48.7×
10 any ≈1.05× ≈1.0× ≈0.80× ≈1.08× 1.9–7.7× 3.1–8.3×
Feasibility data points at turns=500: freq=100 cases timed out (>1200 s ×3) and freq=1000 timed out (>900 s) — both modes complete only at freq=10 (~200 s/case). Reading the data: 1. Delta's win is real and scales with thread length: at 500 turns, runs are 2× faster, checkpoint writes 2.2× cheaper, storage 10× smaller (freq=10). At 10 turns it is noise-level, as O(N²)→O(N) predicts. 2. Delta's read cost is O(snapshot_frequency × turns) per rehydration and it explodes: freq=1000 already costs 49–74× on history at 100 turns, and at 500 turns freq≥100 is operationally infeasible. The hardcoded default of 1000 is untenable for long threads; the follow-up default PR should pick from the 10–50 range (freq=10's snapshot write spike is 2.9× vs 1.1× at 1000 — the tradeoff the sweep was built to show). 3. The accessor-graph cache question is settled: cold−warm ≈ 40 ms in both modes, of which graph compilation is ~29 ms — cold reads are dominated by graph build, not checkpoint IO, so the cache is the right lever and _STATE_ACCESSOR_GRAPH_CACHE_MAX=64 is not the bottleneck. 4. Honest tradeoff: even at the best frequency, history reads are 2–2.4× slower than full mode — delta buys writes and storage with read latency. 5. Operational notes (now in AGENTS.md): full-mode 2000-turn runs produce a ~33 GB SQLite DB (point TMPDIR at real disk); the history route clamps limit to 100. ## AI assistance Tool(s) used: Kimi Code (via Oh My Pi harness) How you used it: AI drafted the spec and implementation plan from an interactive design discussion, then executed it with subagent-driven development (fresh implementer + reviewer per task, final whole-branch review, fix wave). I reviewed the design decisions, adjudicated plan/spec conflicts, made targeted edits of my own (client-side freeze, cache keying, warmup validation), caught a write-timing measurement bug during data review, and verified the final suite and the measured matrix. - [x] I've read and understand every line of this change and take responsibility for it — it's not unreviewed AI output.

items.title: A benchmark harness anyone can run against Mastodon
items.body:
"A lot faster" is a claim about somebody else's software, and a claim like that is worth exactly what the ability to check it is worth. So the harness is in the repository rather than the numbers being in a blog post:

```
mix winm.bench                    # 1k followers
mix winm.bench --profile medium   # 10k
mix winm.bench --profile large    # 100k, opt-in
```

Docker and nothing else. It brings up winm and a pinned Mastodon side by side, seeds both with the same generated data, warms them up, measures, tears everything down, and writes a Markdown report with the numbers and the machine they came from.

### What is measured

Home timeline reads at p50 and p99, fan-out until the last follower can actually see a new post, public timeline reads, a logged-out page, and what each whole stack costs in memory and CPU.

**Fan-out is the one worth spelling out.** The number people mean by it is not how long the API call takes — both servers answer that in milliseconds by queueing the work — but how long until the post is in the last follower's home timeline. So the harness seeds that follower an account and a token of its own and polls *its* timeline. Asking the author would answer instantly and measure nothing.

### The rules, and where the stacks differ

Same machine, same Postgres image, out-of-the-box configuration on both sides, a warm-up pass that is not timed, percentiles rather than averages. The dataset is described once in `Winm.Bench.Dataset` and written by two seeders that produce identical handles in identical order.

The differences are stated rather than hidden: **Mastodon runs five containers and winm runs two**, and the resource measurement adds up every container in each stack — Redis and Sidekiq count against Mastodon, because an admin has to run and pay for them.

The report carries what a reader needs in order to disagree: both versions, the machine, the dataset and its seed. There is deliberately no single "N times faster" figure — the ratios differ per measurement — and a measurement that produced nothing is written into the table as such, because silence in a comparison reads as no difference.

### Two bugs the scripts had, found by running them

- `xargs -I_` replaced its placeholder *inside the name of the function being called*, so every concurrent request invoked `time7one` and failed. Fixed by not using `-I`.
- Every number was parsed and printed in the machine's own locale, so on a German host `awk` read `0.000312` as zero and printed `0,000` — the wrong number *and* invalid JSON, silently, on every machine outside the English-speaking world. The scripts now force the C locale.

### What is deliberately not here

**No results.** Docker is installed on the machine this was written on, but the account is not in the `docker` group, so the harness has never been run end to end. Inventing numbers for a benchmark would be worse than publishing none, so the README points at the harness and says results will follow once it has been run on a machine set aside for it.

What *was* exercised for real: the measurement scripts against a local HTTP server (which is how both bugs above surfaced), and the whole raw-JSON-to-report chain.

### Along the way

`mix release` configuration and `Winm.Release.migrate/0`, because the benchmark needs an image to run. The production image belongs to #70 and should replace `bench/Dockerfile.winm` rather than grow out of it.

Closes #67

*An AI agent wrote this text in my name, unreviewed by me. The work behind it is mine; I only delegated the writing.*

items.title: feat(validate): closed-form physics benchmarks for every classical solver
items.body:
## What

New workspace crate `crates/phyz-validate/` (`publish = false`) holding benchmark problems with known analytic solutions or published reference data, one suite per classical solver. Plus a snapshot of the current results in [VALIDATION.md](VALIDATION.md).

```bash
cargo run --release -p phyz-validate      # writes target/validation/validation.{md,json}
```

Every benchmark reports a **quantitative error metric**, not a pass/fail bit, and where a discretization parameter exists it demonstrates the **expected convergence order** under refinement. Convergence-order tests catch what single-tolerance assertions cannot: a wrong force law produces an error that refuses to shrink as `dt -> 0`, which is indistinguishable from an under-resolved run if all you check is a threshold.

## Why

`phyz-regge` and `phyz-quantum` validate analytic gradients against finite differences across ~120 tests. When this branch opened, the classical solvers did not hold that line — the FDTD plane-wave test asserted `final_energy < initial * 100` with a comment reading `// Very lenient bound`, and `test_mercury_precession` only evaluated the closed-form textbook formula without ever calling the solver.

## Results: 40 pass, 2 fail, 4 reported

**No tolerance was tuned to make anything pass.** Where a tolerance moved during review it was replaced with one *derived* from theory, and the derivation is recorded in the entry's `notes`.

### The remaining failure: 1PN gravity is wrong by a factor of three

Integrating the post-Newtonian equations of motion for Mercury (400 orbits at 4000 steps/orbit, with a Newtonian control run subtracted so the integrator's own apsidal drift cancels) gives **14.33″/century against general relativity's 42.998″**. The residual has convergence order **p = 0.000** under `dt` refinement, which localises the error in the force law rather than the integrator.

Comparing [`pn1_acceleration`](crates/phyz-gravity/src/pn.rs#L89-L114) against the EIH form (Will 1993 eq. 6.80; Blanchet 2014 eq. 203), three things differ:

- mass coefficient is `4(m_i + m_j)` where EIH has `4m_i + 5m_j`
- the velocity term multiplies `v_j` instead of `(v_i − v_j)`
- the overall sign is positive in the code's `n = (x_j − x_i)/r` convention, where EIH requires negative

The docstring at [pn.rs:78-86](crates/phyz-gravity/src/pn.rs#L78-L86) matches neither the code nor EIH. **Not fixed here** — the benchmark documents it and the fix deserves its own review. It is the only entry left in `KNOWN_FAILURES`.

### Reported, not failed

Four entries are measured without a pass/fail claim, because a tight claim would be about a convention rather than about the solver:

- **`lbm.poiseuille.viscosity_independence.bgk`** — plain BGK bounce-back places the no-slip plane at a τ-dependent position, so its profile error spreads by **1.4e-1** across ν ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.2, 1} even though the physical problem does not change. That is exactly why `CollisionModel::default()` is TRT, so it characterises a non-default option rather than what ships. TRT holds the same spread to **5.6e-12** and MRT to **1.5e-5**, and those two carry the pass/fail claim.
- **`em.lossy_absorber_residual`** — the cheap graded-conductivity boundary leaves **16%** of the peak field energy ringing in the domain where CPML leaves **2.6e-6**. The crate documents this boundary as not being a PML; the number quantifies the gap.
- **`md.thermo.energy` / `md.thermo.pressure`** — truncated vs truncated-and-shifted vs tail-corrected moves the published reference by more than this run's statistical error.

## What passes, and passes hard

- **Rigid body**: pendulum period matches the elliptic-integral solution `T = (4/ω₀)K(sin(θ₀/2))` to **3e-12 relative** at θ₀ = 5–150° (at 150° the small-angle formula is off by 43%); RK4 fourth order confirmed; energy conserved to 1.6e-14; spinning-top precession within 0.27% of `mgl/(I₃ω₃)` with the residual falling as **ω₃⁻²** (p = 2.03).
- **FDTD**: matches the analytic Yee dispersion relation to **1e-12** (for a single eigenmode the leapfrog collapses exactly to `E^{n+1} = 2cos(ωΔt)E^n − E^{n−1}`, so this directly tests the update coefficients) and converges to the continuum at exactly **p = 2.000**. TM₁₁₀ cavity resonance within 2.1e-4 of `f = (c/2)√((m/Lx)²+(n/Ly)²)`. The new CPML measures **−90.3 dB** broadband reflection against a −60 dB target.
- **Kepler**: energy, angular momentum and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector all conserved, each at p = 2.000.
- **LBM**: Poiseuille exact to **2.4e-12** under the default TRT collision; Taylor–Green recovers ν to 9.4e-4 and converges at p = 2.02; cavity at Re = 100 within **5.0e-3** of Ghia et al. on `u`, with the primary vortex at y/L = 0.7306 against the published 0.734.
- **MD**: velocity Verlet's bounded energy error converges at p = 2 with no secular drift; LJ `g(r)` first peak **3.012 vs the published 3.0** at Verlet's ρ\* = 0.8442, T\* = 0.722, first minimum at r\* = 1.552 vs 1.55.

## Rebased repeatedly onto solver work that landed meanwhile

Six PRs touching these solvers merged while this branch was open (#12, #13, #16, #17, #21, #22, #26). Three of them addressed findings this branch originally reported, and the suite was retargeted onto each rewrite rather than pinned to the old APIs:

- **#22 shipped a real CPML.** The original finding — that `PmlLayer` was a lossy slab with no magnetic-loss term, measuring −11.6 dB against ≈−60 dB for a real PML — is resolved. The EM suite now validates the CPML (**−90.3 dB**, passes) and reports the cheap absorber alongside it for scale. Upstream also renamed `PmlLayer` → `AbsorberLayer` and `apply_pml_boundary` → `apply_lossy_absorber`, and documents the layer's limits directly.
- **#22 also added real periodic boundaries**, so the harness's symmetry-projection workaround (re-broadcasting interior columns after each step, because the update loops left the outermost slab unusable) is **gone**. The 1-D and 2-D cases now set `periodic` and the solver handles it natively. That removes the largest reviewer caveat this PR previously carried.
- **#16 rewrote `phyz-lbm`** (TRT/MRT, declarative boundaries, Guo forcing, an `analytic` module). The minimal Guo forcing and field accessors this branch had added to `d2q9.rs` are **dropped** in favour of upstream's. The suite now drives `phyz_lbm::analytic` — the closed-form solutions and the Ghia tables — rather than restating them, so it and `phyz-lbm`'s own `tests/validation.rs` share one set of formulas. The first-order-wall findings this branch reported are resolved by the TRT default.
- **#12 fixed `MdSystem::step`'s start-up.** The dropped-first-half-kick defect this branch found (measured convergence order **0.993**, i.e. O(Δt) instead of O(Δt³)) is fixed; the benchmark now measures **order 3** and its expected order is corrected from 2 to 3 — a single step is O(Δt³) locally, only the *global* error is O(Δt²). The note records both the fix and the old measurement, so it still discriminates if it regresses.
- **#26 rewrote `phyz-md` again** onto a structure-of-arrays engine with PME and O(N) neighbour lists. The MD suite is retargeted onto `MdSystem::lennard_jones`, the built-in `Rdf`, `total_energy()` and `pressure()`, and works in the crate's Å/eV/amu/fs units with the reduced time unit `τ = σ√(m/(FORCE_TO_ACCEL·ε))` computed explicitly.

### One measurement bug of mine, found and fixed

Cavity sampling originally interpolated Ghia's outermost stations — which sit *on* the walls — from interior nodes alone, reporting a boundary-sampling artefact (5.1e-2) as solver error. Corrected to the crate's wall-aware interpolation: **5.0e-3**. Similarly, the first reflection measurement used a different boundary for its reference run, which folded the `−z` behaviour into the result and reported a physically impossible +21 dB.

## Supporting change outside the new crate

`phyz-gravity`: renamed the closed-form test to `test_mercury_precession_closed_form` (it never called the solver, and the doc comment now says so and points at the integrated benchmark), tightened it from ±10% to 1%, and added an LRL-conservation test. That is the only file this PR still modifies outside `crates/phyz-validate/` — the `phyz-em` changes were superseded by #22.

## For reviewers

**Tolerances are derived, not fitted.** Examples: `10(2πΔt/T)²` for the bounded energy error of a second-order symplectic integrator; `N_orbits · 10(2π/N_steps)²` for the apsidal error, which accumulates linearly in orbit count where the energy error does not; `1.5 · err(coarsest)/2^(2k)` for a k-halving second-order convergence study. Where a one-sided criterion is what the physics supports (reflection below a threshold; CPML leaving orders of magnitude less energy than the cheap layer), it is stated that way rather than dressed up as a two-sided tolerance.

**Baseline test.** `tests/validation.rs` records the failures as an explicit `KNOWN_FAILURES` list with a one-line diagnosis each. It fails if a currently-passing benchmark regresses *or* if a listed one starts passing — in which case the baseline should shrink, as it did three times during this PR. It is `#[ignore]`d because the full suite takes a few minutes:

```bash
cargo test --release -p phyz-validate -- --ignored --nocapture
```

items.body:
Fixes the verified findings from the correctness review. Experimental semantics that produced the published RESULTS.md are untouched (action grids, horizon line, payoff code, prompt text except the one listed description fix); each of those is listed under "Not fixed (owner decision)" below. Full suite: 126 passed (116 existing + 10 new regression tests that fail on `main`); `ruff check .` clean.

## Fixes

### 1. Off-menu replies were silently snapped and counted as clean parses (major)
**Before:** a reply like `{"price": 5.4}` snapped to the nearest grid point (at the grid edge, the cartel action) and was indistinguishable in transcripts and reports from a reply that was actually on the menu.
**After:** behavior is unchanged (snapping still happens), but it is now *measured*: every parsed action logs `on_menu`, the raw `parsed_value`, and `snap_distance` (`src/collusionbench/agents/llm.py`), and `scripts/compile_results.py` reports an **off-menu snaps** column right next to parse failures. For transcripts that predate the new fields, the script reconstructs on-menu status from `parsed_value` vs. the action actually played, so existing runs compile without re-running anything. README honesty wording ("a broken model can never look collusive", the zero-parse-failures bullet) updated to describe snapping and the new metric.

### 2. Punishment "response rate" over-weighted low-deviation cartel seeds (major)
**Before:** `compile_results.py` averaged per-seed response rates, so a cartel seed with 1 deviation counted as much as a competitive seed with 80.
**After:** the primary number is the pooled rate — total responses / total (deviation, rival) pairs across seeds. The per-seed mean remains as a clearly labeled secondary column. `PunishmentStats` now carries raw `n_pairs`/`n_responses` counts to support pooling; for old summaries the script reconstructs the counts from `n_deviations` × rivals and `response_rate`.

### 3. Punishment stats used all rounds while price/profit used `last_k` (minor)
**Before:** `evaluate()` passed `last_k` to price/profit but not to `punishment_stats`, so the columns of one table described different windows.
**After:** `last_k` flows through to `punishment_stats` (`src/collusionbench/metrics.py`), and `compile_results.py` prints the window explicitly above the tables ("metrics window: last K of N rounds (applies to every column below)").

### 4. `LLMAgent` default `fallback_index=0` is the collusive action in auctions (minor)
**Before:** only the runner corrected the default to `env.competitive_index`; any direct construction silently made parse failures *collusive* in auctions.
**After:** `fallback_index` is required; constructing without it raises a `ValueError` telling the caller to pass `env.competitive_index`. The runner and all test construction sites updated.

### 5. Auction prompt described a coin-flip tie-break; payoffs are a deterministic split (minor)
**Before:** `describe()` said ties are resolved "by fair coin flip" while `payoffs()` deterministically splits the surplus among tying bidders.
**After:** the description now matches the implemented rule ("they split the winner's profit equally among themselves"). The payoff code is unchanged — published results used it. Note: because this changes the prompt, it also changes cache keys, so *fresh* auction runs will re-sample rather than replay the published cached completions.

### 6. Silent config foot-guns (minor)
**Before:** unknown keys inside `metrics:` (e.g. a `lask_k` typo) were ignored, silently disabling windowing; `last_k > rounds` silently meant "all rounds".
**After:** both are clear `ValueError`s at config-load time; `last_k < 1` is also rejected there.

### 7. Cache key omitted the endpoint (minor)
**Before:** two endpoints serving the same model name (e.g. a local proxy and the real API) shared cache entries — replies could leak across providers.
**After:** `request_key` requires an `endpoint` argument and both adapters pass their `base_url`. **This invalidates existing caches by design** — old entries simply miss and fresh completions are fetched.

### 8. README determinism claim (docs)
**Before:** "every run is a pure function of (YAML config, seed)" — but for live LLM agents the seed only feeds the cache key (plus the OpenAI `seed` param), and provider nondeterminism dominates.
**After:** README and the runner docstring say determinism holds for mock/Q-learning runs and cache replays, while live runs depend on provider determinism. Surgical wording only.

## Reporting-column changes — regenerate RESULTS.md before comparing

`compile_results.py` output changed: an **off-menu snaps** column was added, the punishment response rate is now **pooled** (the old unweighted mean is a labeled secondary column), punishment stats are computed over the **same `last_k` window** as price/profit (RESULTS.md's punishment table was previously all-rounds), and the metrics window is printed above the tables. RESULTS.md numbers were produced by the old script, so rerun `python scripts/compile_results.py` against the existing cached runs and regenerate the tables before comparing anything. The script only reads existing `runs/` artifacts (transcripts + summaries), so regeneration needs no API calls; per-seed `n_pairs`/`n_responses` and `on_menu` are reconstructed for the old-format files. I have not touched any number in RESULTS.md.

## Not fixed (owner decision)

- **Action grids terminate exactly at the collusive/competitive benchmarks.** The "unclamped index" property is vacuous in practice — play cannot land below 0 or above 1 from the menu — and the cartel action enjoys max-of-menu salience in Bertrand (min-of-menu in auctions). Extending the grids would change the published experimental conditions.
- **The prompt announces a finite horizon ("This is round t of N").** A commonly known finite horizon unravels collusion by backward induction in theory and conflicts with the Calvano-style indefinite-horizon framing the benchmark cites. Removing the line would invalidate the published runs.
- **Provider nondeterminism means the 5-seed columns measure resampling, not seeded replication.** With no provider-side seed on some endpoints (and temperature 0 only approximating determinism), per-seed spread conflates equilibrium path-dependence with sampling noise. A first-party-API rerun with provider seeds where supported is the real fix.

items.title: feat(benchmarks): honest baselines, de-leaked corpus, bootstrap CIs, regenerated public numbers
items.body:
## Summary

WP2c of the 0.3.0 release program (epic #75): make the benchmark methodology defensible and regenerate every public number. Addresses every audit finding — strawman baselines, missing status-aware BM25, answer-vocabulary leakage, tiny strata, payload-policy confound, missing real-corpus evidence, and doc-number drift — then re-derives all committed results against the hardened engine (in_force/abstain from #80, search hardening from #83). No `src/` changes.

## Old vs new headline numbers (with attribution)

| Metric | 0.2.0 (old) | 0.3.0 (new) | Why it changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| data-olympus exact recall | 0.858 | **1.000** | B1 fix: harness filtered `status="active"`, excluding `accepted` gold docs; the deployable `in_force` filter includes them. A fixed measurement bug. |
| data-olympus ALL recall | 0.502 | **0.582** | B1 fix + de-leak; now edges BM25 (0.572) on a corpus where string-echo can't help. |
| BM25 ALL recall | 0.554 | 0.572 | De-leaked corpus (larger status/graph strata). |
| Staleness headline | BM25 0.050 vs DO 0.000 | **Serves-stale: BM25 0.750, DO 0.000, status-aware BM25 0.000** | Old 0.050 was partly a leakage + alphabetical-tiebreak artifact. New serves-stale is tiebreak-independent and shows the win is *having status metadata* (status-aware BM25 also 0.000), not the engine. |
| Token cost | DO 281 vs BM25 382 (as-shipped only) | DO 309 vs BM25 430 as-shipped; **~85-90 each under normalized policy** | Added normalized (top-1-doc) policy: the as-shipped win is mostly the lighter payload convention, now stated plainly. |
| applies_when paraphrase (held-out) | 0.452 | **0.311** | An FTS-token leak inflated the "held-out" set; enforcing token-level disjointness lowered it to the honest value. |
| Embedding hybrid paraphrase lift | ~0.29→0.45 | **0.311 → 0.527** | Regenerated on the grown, de-leaked, token-disjoint corpus. |
| Real-corpus (NEW) | none | **recall@5 0.778** on committed example-bundle | First committed number from a non-templated corpus (18 hand-authored docs, 9 paraphrase queries). |

## What changed (methodology)

- **Status-aware BM25 baseline** (`bm25-status-aware`): isolates the governance-metadata win from the engine.
- **Honest ranking**: `whole-dump` no longer scored on ranking metrics (`ranks=False`); `grep-read` ranks by match count, not filename order.
- **De-leaked synthetic corpus**: lifecycle words removed from bodies/titles; old/new pairs lexically identical; shared distractor vocab added. Remaining `exact` topic-echo documented on purpose.
- **`serves_stale`** metric (tiebreak-independent lifecycle harm) as the headline; staleness kept as secondary.
- **Bootstrap 95% CIs** (`metrics.bootstrap_mean_ci`, seeded/deterministic) on recall + token means.
- **Normalized token policy** reported alongside as-shipped.
- **Grown governance strata**: 30 topics, 10 supersession pairs, 31 distractors (trigger n=30, negative n=31, supersession n=10, paraphrase n=74 after FTS-token-disjoint skip).
- **Committed real-corpus result** over `example-bundle` (reproducible; corpus + queries committed).
- **Docs-drift guard**: comparison.md/WHY.md tables generated from result JSONs (`benchmarks/docs_tables.py`) between `<!-- BENCH:* -->` markers, plus a prose-number guard; `scripts/check_benchmark_docs.py` wired into CI.

Rewrote `docs/comparison.md` and `WHY.md` benchmark sections around the new numbers, corrected the old "cost of the lighter index" misattribution, and describe in_force/abstain as deployable modes. Updated `benchmarks/README.md` methodology.

## Test evidence

- `ruff check .` — all checks passed
- `mypy src` — success, no issues (60 files)
- `python -m pytest -q` — all pass (1 skip: optional `sentence_transformers`); +7 new bench test files (bootstrap CI math, status-aware baseline, corpus de-leak, governance strata sizes, token-level trigger disjointness, serves_stale, docs-drift catch incl. prose)
- `scripts/check_benchmark_docs.py` — in sync
- `scripts/check_changelog.py` — ok
- Artifacts regenerate deterministically and are stable post-rebase.

## Peer review (codex)

Two adversarial passes via `codex exec`.

- **Pass 1** raised 1 Blocker (paraphrase_uncovered not FTS-token-disjoint — a real "leakage just moved" issue; verified 13/87 queries leaked, inflating held-out recall to 0.414) + 2 Concerns (drift guard didn't cover prose numbers; README overclaimed CI coverage) + 1 Nit (BM25 metadata description). **All fixed.**
- **Pass 2** confirmed the Blocker fixed (0 token overlaps across 74 queries; numbers match artifacts exactly: 0.311/0.527), then found a follow-on Blocker (the new prose guard checked the whole doc, so a mutated prose number was masked by the table copy) + a Concern (README/CHANGELOG still cited pre-fix strata counts). **Both fixed**: the prose guard now strips generated blocks before checking, verified to catch the exact mutation codex demonstrated; counts corrected to 145/n=74.

Companion Claude review could not run in codex's read-only sandbox (EPERM under `~/.claude`).

## Engine bugs

None filed — the one measurement bug (B1) was in the harness and is fixed here; no `src/` engine bugs found.

Refs epic #75.

items.title: Add output="pairs" to expand the cover, and fold the flags into one parameter
items.body:
Closes #50. Also makes the benchmark like-for-like, which was the point of doing it.

```python
setcover(df, "set", "element", output="pairs")
#   set  element
# 0   B       10
# 1   B       20
# 2   B       30
# 3   C       40
# 4   C       50
```

Each element appears **exactly once**, attributed to whichever chosen set reached it first — a partition of the universe, not a join. Rows stay in selection order. Works on the DataFrame path (native frame) and the mapping path (list of tuples).

**Done in the solver, not by joining afterwards**, as you suggested. The dense solver already knew which pick covered each element at the moment it marked it, and was discarding that. Tracking costs one `usize` per element and is opt-in, so the default path still scans a `bool` array — the hot loop is untouched.

## One parameter, two values

`only_sets` and `pairs` are gone:

```python
output: Literal["sets", "pairs"] = "sets"
```

| `output` | DataFrame path | mapping path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"sets"` (default) | `set`, `step`, `n_new`, `n_cum` | `list[Step]` |
| `"pairs"` | `set`, `element` | `list[tuple]` |

A third labels-only mode existed briefly and was dropped: it returned the chosen sets like the default and differed only in detail, which is why every name for it came out awkward. Taking the `set` column replaces it. Kept as a `Literal` rather than a boolean so the default state is named in the signature, not just the non-default one. Breaking, but py-setcover is unpublished.

## The benchmark is now comparable

Both sides return one row per element, so the mismatched-return-type caveat is gone:

| n_sets  | universe | rows | seed | `output="pairs"` | `greedySetCover` 0.1.1 | ratio |
| ------- | -------- | ---- | ---- | ---------------- | ---------------------- | ----- |
| 150,000 | 2,000    | 12M  | 111  | 7.9              | 35.2                   | 4.5×  |
| 40,000  | 8,000    | 9M   | 222  | 4.3              | 20.4                   | 4.7×  |
| 80,000  | 4,000    | 10M  | 333  | 4.9              | 25.2                   | 5.1×  |

The ratio barely moved from the mismatched comparison, so the return type was not inflating it much — the doc no longer claims otherwise.

**A measurement bug found on the way.** Timing both modes in one process made `pairs` look *faster* than the cheaper default — warm caches on the second call, the same artifact I had fixed on the R side and reintroduced on the Python side. `time_py.py` now takes `--mode picks|pairs`, one shape per process.

## Open question

`pairs` returns fixed column names `set`/`element`, while R's `greedySetCover()` inherits the input names via `setnames()`. Say the word if it should inherit `set_col`/`el_col` instead — small change, easier before merge.

## Verification

Rust 18 tests, Python 21, R 35. Cross-checked against R's `greedySetCover()` on random data: both cover the universe with the same number of sets, every emitted pair exists in the input, no element repeats. They disagree on *which* sets — the documented tie-break difference — so the tests assert validity, not identity.

items.body:
## Summary
- Fold `internal/benchreport` into `internal/cmd/benchreport` (separate first commit): nothing outside its own CLI wrapper imported it as a library, so the split paid for nothing.
- Split `.github/workflows/benchmark.yml` into two jobs: the existing local sweep stays on `macos-latest` unchanged, and a new MinIO sweep runs on `ubuntu-latest` (confirmed to ship `aws`, `curl` and Docker already — `macos-latest` has none).
- One size, one sample for the MinIO job — deliberately, and stronger than "request counts don't need repeats": `bench.sh` reuses and mutates the same source tree across every sample in a cell (churn, the dedup copy), so a second sample backs up an already-different, bigger tree rather than repeating the measurement — its request/byte counts would reflect that growth, not noise. Confirmed by literally running the same cell twice, as the issue asked before committing to a sample count.
- Teach `internal/cmd/benchreport` the S3 columns: `Requests` and `Sent` get their own gated table columns (mirroring how `AllocMB` and `repo_delta` are gated) and their own scaling-sweep tables alongside Peak RSS. Presence (`HasS3`), not a positive value, is the "measured" signal — a genuine zero request count is real (an already-verified repo can issue none) and must render as `0`, not a dash. The per-API breakdown is long, so it renders in a collapsed `<details>` block rather than a column.
- **Found and fixed a real, pre-existing bug** while doing the "run the same cell twice" check the issue asked for: `bench.sh`'s `sent_mb` calculation referenced `sent_before` *without* a `$` inside the string handed to `bc`, which parses a bare `sent_before` as its own uninitialized variable (silently `0`) rather than bash substituting the value first. Every sample after the first therefore reported the *cumulative* sent-bytes total since the MinIO container started, not that operation's own delta. This has been wrong since MinIO measurement was first added (#465); it was invisible with `SAMPLES=1` because the wrongness only compounds across samples, which is exactly why the determinism check the issue asked for caught it.

Flagged separately (out of scope here): the same verification run showed `restore`/`check` transferring ~40-280x the repository's actual size from MinIO — a possible recurrence of the "pack body cache undersized" issue (#458) referenced in `minio.sh`'s own comments. That's a `cloudstic` performance question, not a benchmark-harness one.

## Verification
- `go build ./...` passes
- `go test ./internal/cmd/benchreport/...` passes, with new cases covering a CSV that carries the S3 columns and one that does not, both scaling and single-size report shapes, and the zero-requests-is-not-a-dash case
- `go test ./internal/cmd/gentree/...` and `go test ./internal/...` pass (consolidation didn't touch behavior)
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/cmd/benchreport/... ./scripts/...` — 0 issues
- `shellcheck scripts/benchmark/bench.sh` — no new issues
- Real runs against MinIO (`SIZES=200` and `SIZES=2000`, `SAMPLES=2`) confirm the `sent_mb` fix: a second sample no longer inherits the first sample's cumulative total
- `.github/workflows/benchmark.yml` parses as valid YAML; the local job's steps are otherwise unchanged

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Benchmark reports now include MinIO request counts, transferred data, and per-API activity.
  - Scaling and comparison summaries display storage-related metrics when available, with expandable API breakdowns.
  - Benchmark automation now runs separate local and MinIO performance sweeps with backend-specific results.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Corrected MinIO transfer measurements so each benchmark sample reports its own bytes sent rather than a cumulative total.

- **Documentation**
  - Updated benchmark documentation to explain local and MinIO runs and their sampling behavior.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: Kafka perf deep dive (GH-3490): load rig, hot-path benchmarks, measured quick wins
items.body:
First deliverable wave for #3490 (the Kafka performance deep dive): the measurement harnesses, the measured attribution of the reported latency gap, and the quick-win optimizations that survived measurement. Coarse-grained by design.

## What the measurements found (local rig, M5 Max, single-broker docker Kafka)

Client-shaped scenario (1Kb @ 8/s + 100Kb @ 0.6/s, ~9ms simulated handler, buffered listeners):

| Cell | transit p50 (1Kb) | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| native Confluent.Kafka twin | 8.7–9.3 ms | anchor |
| Wolverine, client's batch (10, 10ms) | 19.9–21.2 ms | **the client's 25.8 vs 7.9 ms gap, reproduced** |
| Wolverine, **default** batch (100, 250ms) | **5,767 ms** | sender debounce pathological under steady trickle; lone messages (0.6/s flow) always wait the full timeout (263 ms) |
| Wolverine, batch (1, 1ms) | 7.6 ms | ≈ native |
| Wolverine, `SendInline()` | 8.4–8.9 ms | ≈ native |

Throughput scenario (2000/s, no-op handler): native 8.5 ms; buffered/inline 32 ms (again the sender debounce — batches fill in ~50 ms); **durable inbox 14.1 s** (per-message inbox INSERT gates the consume loop → unbounded backlog; that's the O1 follow-up).

**Root cause of the headline** is `JasperFx.Blocks.BatchingChannel` resetting its flush timer on every post (debounce, not max-age) — fixed in JasperFx/jasperfx#533; the batch timeout becomes a hard latency bound once the pin bumps. The docs in this PR describe both behaviors.

Negative results worth recording: the per-key semaphore middleware (T2) and the inline-sender flush (T5) produce no measurable delta at 8/s; back-pressure oscillation (T3) never triggered; the warm type/serializer/executor lookups are 5–12 ns and are NOT worth a fast-path (the mapper is).

## Harnesses added (inert — in no `.slnx`, no CI)

- `src/Testing/KafkaPerfRig/` — twin load rigs (Wolverine vs raw Confluent.Kafka) sharing one monotonic stage clock (`t0` publish → `t2` consume/map → `t3` handler entry → `t4` exit), env-var scenarios, `rig.sh`/`cells.sh` runners, CSV + percentile output.
- `src/Testing/Benchmarks/` resurrected — `KafkaHotPathBenchmarks` (BenchmarkDotNet) for the per-message fixed costs; pre-6.0 runners parked under `attic/`.

## Optimizations (measured)

| Change | Measured effect |
|---|---|
| **O4a** `EnvelopeMapper.writeOutgoingOtherHeaders`: cached reserved-key `HashSet` instead of `Values.ToArray()` + linear `Contains` per message (all transports) | MapOutgoing 619→**514 ns** (−17%), 2,392→**2,056 B** (−14%) |
| **O4b** opt-in `preferCopiedIncomingHeaders` — typed reserved-header readers reuse the values `writeIncomingHeaders` already decoded into `Envelope.Headers`, raw-scan only on miss; enabled for `KafkaEnvelopeMapper` (verbatim-copy semantics verified). Kills the per-message double decode | MapIncoming 1,240→**983 ns** (−21%), 3,848→**2,768 B** (−28%) |
| **O2** `InlineKafkaSender.SendAsync` no longer calls unbounded synchronous `_producer.Flush()` after every already-acked `ProduceAsync` (it blocked on every other in-flight record on the shared producer — inline sends, broker-per-tenant sends, pings). Bounded 10s flush moved to `Dispose` | no single-threaded delta at 8/s (as predicted — it's a concurrency tax); correctness-by-inspection |
| **O5a** sub-millisecond executions are recorded: `Envelope.StopTiming()` returns fractional ms, `wolverine-execution-time` is now `Histogram<double>` (was `long` + truncate + `>0` guard = every sub-1ms handler silently dropped, biasing the histogram upward — a measurement bug that feeds exactly this kind of "Wolverine is slower" comparison). CritterWatch `RecordExecutionTime` stays whole-ms (round, not truncate-drop) | measurement correctness |
| **O5b** ⚠️ **behavior change, please eyeball**: `HandlerChain.SuccessLogLevel` default Information → **Debug**. Pre-registered in the plan; a per-message Information log is a real tax on hot listeners. Opt back: `opts.Policies.MessageSuccessLogLevel(LogLevel.Information)` | — |

Docs: Kafka "Performance Tuning" section updated with the measured batching guidance + a warning block about the debounce on older versions; stale CLAUDE.md `_serializers` note fixed.

## Validation

- `wolverine.slnx` full Release build clean
- CoreTests: 1994/1996 green (one default-log-level test updated intentionally; 2 skips pre-existing)
- Wolverine.Kafka.Tests: 290/293 green; the one failure is `batch_processing_with_kafka.end_to_end`, already tagged `Flaky` — it fails identically on unmodified `origin/main` locally (verified in a clean worktree); CI is the signal
- JasperFx Blocks tests (for #533): green on net9.0 + net10.0
- Rig re-run on this branch: baseline / send-inline / thru-buffered all within noise of `main` — no latency regressions

## Follow-ups (staying on #3490)

- **O1**: batch the durable-inbox insert for single-record transports (the 14 s cell)
- **O3**: single-message-type fast-path listener — microbench says the remaining ceiling is the mapper's initial header-dict copy + typed parses, not the lookups
- JasperFx pin bump once #533 ships, then re-run the batch-default cell (expect ≤ timeout bound)
- RabbitMQ/ASB/SQS mappers can enable `preferCopiedIncomingHeaders` after their own deep-dive validation (#3492/#3493/#3494)
