items.title: fix: run benchmarks on the baked toolchain, and let a non-root sandbox use the baked artifacts
items.body: Every Runloop cell in [run 31009659726](https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks/actions/runs/31009659726) failed except `disk`, `network` and `system`. It reads as "Runloop is flaky." It isn't: it's one repo-wide measurement bug plus three leaves that assume the identity which *baked* the image is the identity *running* it. Runloop (uid 4444) is simply the only provider that can't paper over them. ## 1. Every provider has been benchmarking the wrong toolchain `setup.ts` and `pins.ts` each carry node/pnpm/mise, coupled by a comment. #243 bumped the pins on 2026-07-21 (node 22.22.3 → 22.23.1, pnpm 10.34.3 → 10.34.5) and left `setup.ts` behind. Every version check in `setup.ts` is EXACT, so since then the baked toolchain has MISSED on every provider and every sandbox: the fallback downloads node 22.22.3 and runs `mise use --global`, which — because the image sets `MISE_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/mise` — rewrites the image's own `config.toml`, header (`do not edit by hand`) and all. The four `setupNode` suites have been measuring a runtime-fetched toolchain rather than the pinned one. That is silent wherever the sandbox user is root. On Runloop the write is denied, so the step failed 3/3 attempts and took all 12 replicates of `cpu-node` and the three `realworld` suites with it. Measured on a live devbox: shipped constants → exit 1 in 989 ms with the CI error verbatim; aligned constants → **exit 0 in 696 ms, nothing installed**. **Leaderboard note:** the four node suites now measure node 22.23.1 / pnpm 10.34.5 instead of 22.22.3 / 10.34.3. Provider-vs-provider rankings in existing data stay valid — every provider got the same wrong node, so it was a level shift, not a skew — but numbers before and after this PR come from different toolchains, and nothing in the committed dataset records which. Worth a fresh matrix run. ## 2. Three leaves resolved the install tree by the wrong path `$(pts_user_dir)/installed-tests` is the install root only by coincidence: for root, PTS's daemonized branch forces `pts_user_dir` to `/var/lib`. Unprivileged it moves to `$HOME` while the baked tests stay behind — the case `pts_install_root()` exists to express. - **`memory/stream`** — hard failure. `cd: .../stream-1.3.4: No such file or directory`, 3/3 replicates. - **`network/iperf-wan`** — *silent*. `rm -f` and `[ -f ]` on an impossible path both no-op, so the suite stayed green while the WAN provenance the leaf calls uninterpretable-without went missing. The run artifacts have `pts_iperf-wan--server-choices.ndjson` for all three e2b replicates and none for runloop. - **`network/fast-cli`** — same bug, dormant leaf. Fixed rather than left as a live twin. Proven inert for root providers, from the run logs: e2b stages profiles at `/var/lib/phoronix-test-suite/…` with the install root at `/var/lib/phoronix-test-suite/installed-tests` — the same tree — while runloop stages at `/home/user/.phoronix-test-suite/…`. ## 3. Baked artifacts a non-root user can write but not own `25-pts-profiles.sh` leaves the tree `a+rwX`, which is enough to create, truncate and delete — and not enough to `chmod`, which is gated on ownership. So the stream recompile rewrote the launcher successfully and then died `EPERM` on the file it had just written. `claim_baked_profile_dir` takes ownership first, falling back to the stock-image discard-and-reinstall branch when there is no sudo. `pgbench` is the same theme with two layers: the bake initdb's as root and must re-tighten `pg_/data/db` to 0700 (postgres FATALs on any group/other bit), so an unprivileged user can't read the data dir — `pg_ctl` never starts — and once it can, the profile's generated script passes no `-U` anywhere, so libpq defaults to an OS username with no role. That's the opaque `pgbench: error: could not create connection for setup`. `claim_baked_pg_cluster` claims the dir and exports `PGUSER` taken from the pre-chown owner, which IS initdb's user. It claims rather than re-initdb's, because a runtime initdb would vary encoding/locale per provider and pgbench only compares across the same cluster. ## 4. A gate, so this class can't recur silently `toolchain-runtime-pins.test.ts` ties the two pin copies together (text-extracted both sides, following `pts-profile-pins` rather than pulling a workspace dep into repo-checks). Mutation-checked: restoring `NODE_VERSION = "22.22.3"` fails it with `Expected "22.23.1" / Received "22.22.3"` and nothing else. It also pins the *exactness* of the version check, since every other assertion would pass against a fuzzy `node@22` — the same bug in disguise. It covers `PTS_VERSION` too, which was a live fourth instance. ## Verification — real sandboxes, not reasoning | suite | before | runloop now | e2b (root control) | |---|---|---|---| | `cpu-node` | 12/12 failed | validated | — | | `realworld-better-auth` | 12/12 failed | validated, 10 metrics | — | | `memory` | 3/3 failed | validated, 4 metrics | validated | | `pgbench` | 3/3 failed | **validated, first numbers ever** | validated | | `network` | green, provenance missing | validated + provenance | validated | Root-provider deltas vs the committed run: pgbench +0.2%…+4.1%. STREAM came back +9%, so I measured the spread — three replicates of the same code on e2b vary 2.9–11.1%, with the committed values within 0.4% of the observed minimum. Noise, not regression. `memory` and `pgbench` were re-run again after the `/simplify` refactor, since it touched already-proven paths. ## Not done, deliberately - `realworld-mastra` and `realworld-openclaw` were not run. They fail and are fixed by the identical `setupNode` path that `cpu-node` and `better-auth` both prove, but that's an inference, not a measurement. - Three deeper restructures the review surfaced: hoisting the pins into `packages/schema` so alignment holds by construction (the `PTS_APT_DEPS` precedent — strongest of the three); `rm -f`-before-heredoc in the vendored install scripts, which would delete `claim_baked_profile_dir` entirely; and writing the bootstrap role at bake time. All are outside this diff's footprint. --- ## Summary by cubic Run benchmarks against the baked toolchain and let non‑root sandboxes use baked artifacts safely. Fixes Runloop failures, adds a drift gate to keep runtime pins aligned with the image, and ensures `pgbench` and STREAM skip or reinstall cleanly when recovery isn’t possible. - **Bug Fixes** - Aligned `node`, `pnpm`, `mise`, and `PTS` pins in `packages/harness/src/lib/setup.ts` with the baked pins; kept exact version checks and added `$SUDO` only to the `mise` fallback. - Resolved PTS paths using `pts_install_root` instead of `pts_user_dir`; fixed `network/iperf-wan` provenance clearing and `network/fast-cli` launcher repair. - For `memory/stream`, claim the baked dir before in‑place repair and guard against stale binaries; if the dir can’t be claimed, discard the baked install to force a fresh PTS reinstall, asserting the discard lands and writing a failure marker if it doesn’t. - For `pgbench`, `claim_baked_pg_cluster` now exports `PGUSER` from the bootstrap owner, records it beside the data dir, and writes skip markers for both modes when sudo isn’t available or the role cannot be recovered, avoiding opaque libpq failures. - **Refactors** - Added `tooling/repo-checks/src/toolchain-runtime-pins.test.ts` to prevent pin drift between bake and runtime; asserts exact checks remain and includes `PTS_VERSION`. - Consolidated elevation and claiming logic in `lib/bench.sh`; unified sudo detection and skip handling. Written for commit 5109e39ad8a0d589b22dfd94f620a266f9aadba1. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved benchmark reliability when using preinstalled test profiles and PostgreSQL clusters in non-root environments. * Added safe fallback installation when existing benchmark assets cannot be claimed. * Skips PostgreSQL benchmarks when required permission repair is unavailable. * **Chores** * Updated fallback versions for mise, Node.js, and pnpm. * Improved setup permissions so only system-level tooling requires elevation. * **Tests** * Added checks to keep runtime versions and checksums synchronized across project configurations.

items.title: Add automatic GPU telemetry sampling for benchmark runs
items.body:
`vram_gb` and `power_w` were always `null` — nobody watches Task Manager during a run. This samples them on the Windows box for the duration of a run and records **peak and mean separately**, since peak sizes the card and mean drives energy cost.

## No third-party sensor library needed

The premise going in was that power would need LibreHardwareMonitor, HWiNFO64 or AMD SMI. It doesn't.

Windows genuinely has no board-power counter — confirmed on the box: the GPU counter sets carry memory and utilisation only, and `Win32_PerfFormattedData_PowerMeterCounter_PowerMeter` has **no instances** (the Energy Meter API is a battery/laptop facility). But `atiadlxx.dll` — AMD's ADL, which ships with the Radeon driver — is already present and exposes board power via plain C exports. **No install, no admin, no service, no registry change.** It's the same API LibreHardwareMonitor wraps internally.

| option | verdict |
|---|---|
| LibreHardwareMonitor | works, but a DLL to deploy + ring-0 driver wants admin; it reads AMD power *through ADL* anyway |
| HWiNFO64 | not open source, shared-memory gated behind paid tier, wants a resident process |
| AMD SMI | not present; Linux/datacentre-focused, consumer RDNA3 on Windows unsupported |
| **AMD ADL** ✅ | already on the box, no admin, no install |

## The power sensor was identified empirically

RDNA3 leaves the expected slots unsupported (`ASIC_POWER`=23, `GFX_POWER`=30). Rather than guess, all 256 slots were logged across an idle→load transition:

```
slot   idle   load   identification
s1       11   2677   gfx clock MHz  (7800 XT boost range)
s19       1     99   GPU activity %
s40       3      3   PCIe gen  ) these two pin the enum
s41      16     16   PCIe lanes)  alignment independently
s73      24    133   ** BOARD POWER W **
```

## Verification — idle vs loaded, 60 s each

| metric | idle | loaded |
|---|---|---|
| power peak / mean | 51 W / 40.5 W | **146 W / 102.4 W** |
| GPU activity peak / mean | 5% / 3.1% | **100% / 55.3%** |
| gfx clock peak | 93 MHz | **2706 MHz** |
| energy | 0.68 Wh | **1.72 Wh** |
| VRAM peak | 15.459 GB | 15.372 GB |

VRAM deliberately does **not** differ — LM Studio keeps the model resident, so VRAM measures what's loaded, not what's working. Documented, because it looks like a bug otherwise.

## Three measurements that shaped the implementation

- **`Get-Counter` costs ~1010 ms per call** (it takes two samples to cook rate counters) — unusable at a 1000 ms interval. The CIM raw classes return the same data in 12–37 ms, so the sampler reads those and does its own delta arithmetic. Steady state: ~66–76 ms/sample, ~7% of one core, **zero GPU work**.
- **Summing every GPU engine is misleading.** With the GPU otherwise idle it read ~50%, because a browser was decoding video at 47% of the Video Codec Engine. Scoped to 3D+Compute: 2.04%, matching ADL exactly. Both are reported, separately named, and the "quiet GPU" protocol rule now covers background video.
- **Windows sshd puts session children in a job object**, so a `Start-Process` worker is killed the instant the `ssh` command returns. The worker is launched via `Win32_Process.Create` instead.

## Safety properties (each was a bug first)

- The worker **publishes its own PID**. Inferring it from the process tree is racy — it latched onto a transient sibling and the reap terminated the wrong process. Nothing is now killed without re-verifying the target's command line names this script, this run id *and* `-Worker`.
- `-MaxRunSec` valve (default 2 h) so a crashed harness can't leave a sampler running forever; `-Start` reaps a stale worker for the same run id.
- The uninstall script's process filter would have **matched and killed its own query process** — fixed.

## Other notes

- Unavailable sensors emit `null`, never `0` — the schema treats them as different facts.
- Telemetry failure never fails a benchmark; it degrades to `gpu_telemetry: null`.
- pt-BR box: the worker pins `InvariantCulture` so no decimal comma reaches the JSON, and the one privilege check uses the SID `S-1-5-32-544`.
- Paths use `%USERPROFILE%` / `$env:USERPROFILE`, no hardcoded username, since this is a public repo others point at their own server.
- Uninstall sends PowerShell via `-EncodedCommand`; as a plain `-Command` string, multi-line pipelines were mangled by cmd.exe.

## Open items (why this is a draft)

- `benchmarks/results.jsonl` is **not** in this PR. It has 2 `--limit 2` validation rows from my testing (labelled in `notes`) mixed with your in-flight aider-polyglot rows — your call whether to keep them.
- Your uncommitted aider-polyglot / cloud-baseline work in `run_bench.py`, `benchmarks/README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` is deliberately excluded; this branch is built on `origin/main` so those files will need a trivial merge.
- Board power is the card's own telemetry, not cross-checked against a wall meter. It also excludes CPU-side cost, which is material given the 30B partially offloads.

items.title: feat(recall): set keyword ranking weight from benchmark data (v2.32.0)
items.body:
v2.31.0 activated keyword candidates for natural-language recall but left keyword scores out of ranking, because the old 0.35 weight had been chosen while that path never ran. This sweeps it and turns it on.

Defaults, both measured on LoCoMo (1,977 questions, 5,882 memories, top-5):
- HYBRID_SEARCH_TEXT_WEIGHT 0.0 -> 0.05. Swept over 13 points; any-hit peaks across a broad 0.04-0.08 plateau at 62.0-62.5% against 57.4% with keyword scoring off and 57.6% at the old 0.35. 0.05 is the plateau centre rather than the argmax, so the default is not fitted to one corpus. High weights are actively harmful: single-hop falls 56.9% -> 47.3% between 0.05 and 0.35.
- FTS_CANDIDATE_LIMIT 50 -> 200. This was the lever on the multi-hop regression v2.31.0 introduced; 200 recovers multi-hop any-hit 34.8% -> 39.3%, matching the pre-v2.31.0 baseline, lifts single-hop 1.1pp, leaves adversarial precision unchanged, and costs ~3ms per recall. 500 buys 1.1pp more multi-hop but erodes the adversarial gain, since a pool that large stops narrowing anything.

Combined vs v2.31.0 on the same corpus: any-hit 57.4% -> 62.5%, all-hit 47.6% -> 52.6%, evidence recall 51.9% -> 56.9%. Every category improves.

Also fixes non-reproducible candidate selection, found because two identical benchmark runs scored 0.5pp apart while disagreeing on 18 questions. Ties at the candidate cutoff are the normal case (53.7% of queries) and SQLite ordered those rows differently between processes, so the pool varied across restarts. Candidate selection now breaks ties on memory ID. Accuracy is unchanged within measurement error; results are now reproducible, which also drops the benchmark's resolution floor from ~0.5pp to ~0.1pp. The fusion bake-off compares methods that can differ by less than the old floor, so it could not have been measured on the previous harness.

New setting FTS_LONE_HIT_SCORE (default 1.0) sets the keyword score for a candidate set too degenerate to rank. It ships as a no-op: swept over 0.0/0.3/0.5/1.0 with no measurable effect, because only 1 of 1,982 queries produced such a set on a store this size. Exposed for small stores, where a query matching exactly one memory is routine. The spec had called the previous hardcoded 1.0 an active ranking bug; measurement says otherwise, since under wide OR a degenerate set means one memory held the only match for any query term, which is discriminative rather than weak evidence.

No schema change, no migration, no re-embedding. Recall ordering changes by design; explicit env overrides are unaffected.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Improved keyword/semantic ranking with updated default weighting.
  * Increased the default keyword candidate limit from 50 to 200.
  * Added `FTS_LONE_HIT_SCORE` to control scoring for single/tied keyword matches.
  * Retrieval diagnostics now display the single-match score.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Made keyword candidate selection deterministic on tie scores for consistent results across runs.
* **Documentation**
  * Updated configuration, FAQ, and installation materials to reflect v2.32.0 and the new default settings.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.6.0...v1.6.1)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance (123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings)

##### Performance — gjson-style fast-skip in hot loops

Ported gjson's `>'\\'` fast-skip trick to three inner loops in parser.go:
`stringEndConfig` tail, `blockEndConfig`, and `searchKeysConfig`. The trick
uses a single unsigned comparison (`byte > 0x5C`) to skip all non-structural

| Payload        | Before    | After         | Improvement |

parser like jsonparser) and [bytedance/sonic](https://redirect.github.com/bytedance/sonic)
(9.6k⭐, SIMD-accelerated deserializer) to the benchmark suite.

**Final leaderboard (large payload):**

| Library              | time/op    | bytes/op | allocs/op |
| -------------------- | ---------- | -------- | --------- |
| **buger/jsonparser** | **20,114** | **0**    | **0**     |

| encoding/json        | 130,565    | 4,432    | 147       |

jsonparser is **the fastest across all payload sizes** and the **only zero-allocation** parser.

***

### [`v1.6.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v160--2026-07-29)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.5.1...v1.6.0)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance (123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings)

##### New API — `Append`

```go
// Append to an array without knowing its length
data, _ = jsonparser.Append(data, []byte(`"new_item"`), "items")
```

- **`Append(data, value, keys...)`** — appends `value` to the end of the JSON array addressed by `keys`. Addresses the top-level value when `keys` is empty; auto-vivifies a missing keyed path as a single-element array. Returns `MalformedArrayError` when the addressed value is not an array. Traced to SYS-REQ-009, SYS-REQ-110.

##### Known issues — all resolved (zero open)

- **KI-2 fixed** — `ParseInt("-")` now returns an error instead of `(0, nil)`. One-line sign-only guard in `bytes.go:parseInt` (after stripping the sign byte, an empty remainder returns `(0, false, false)`).
- **KI-3 fixed** — `Set` with an array-index path component under an object parent (and vice-versa) now auto-coerces the container type instead of emitting malformed JSON. (Disposition already set to `fixed` in v1.5.x.)
- **KI-4 fixed** — `Set` on a top-level array-index beyond length now appends at the array's end (matching nested-array behavior under SYS-REQ-110) instead of returning `KeyPathNotFoundError`. Also cleans up trailing commas in malformed arrays.

**Zero open known issues.** Every previously shipped known issue is now resolved and covered by ReqProof L3 Assurance.

***

### [`v1.5.1`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v151--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.5.0...v1.5.1)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance (123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings)

##### Performance — 6.1x large-payload speedup

- **Fix stringEnd unbounded backslash scan** — `stringEndConfig` was scanning the ENTIRE remaining parent document for backslashes (`bytes.IndexByte(data, '\\')`) instead of just the string body. On a 24kb large payload this walked tens of KB per string. Now bounded to `data[:firstQuote]` (the string body only). **128µs → 22µs (5.8x).**
- **SWAR string scan** — replaced two separate `bytes.IndexByte` calls (quote + backslash) with a single inline 8-byte SWAR (SIMD-Within-A-Register) loop that checks for both characters simultaneously. **22µs → 21µs (additional 8%).**
- **Benchmark suite updated** — all comparison libraries (gabs, easyjson, ffjson, etc.) updated to latest versions. Benchmark methodology documented (Apple M4 Max, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs). The `encoding/json` benchmark no longer uses ffjson-generated methods (the [#​126](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/126) ffjson measurement bug was fixed in v1.3.1).
- **README benchmarks refreshed** — all numbers now reflect real measurements on modern hardware with current library versions.

##### Updated benchmark results (Apple M4 Max, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs)

| Payload                 | jsonparser | encoding/json | easyjson  | Speedup vs encoding/json |
| ----------------------- | ---------- | ------------- | --------- | ------------------------ |
| Small (190B, Get)       | 382 ns     | 1,335 ns      | 312 ns    | 3.5x                     |
| Small (190B, EachKey)   | 241 ns     | —             | —         | 5.5x                     |
| Medium (2.4kB, Get)     | 3,894 ns   | 10,564 ns     | 2,444 ns  | 2.7x                     |
| Medium (2.4kB, EachKey) | 1,923 ns   | —             | —         | 5.5x                     |
| Large (24kB)            | 20,788 ns  | 134,123 ns    | 32,765 ns | **6.4x**                 |

All jsonparser results: **0 bytes allocated, 0 allocations**.

***

### [`v1.5.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v150--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.4.0...v1.5.0)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance

v1.5.0 extends the formal-verification coverage to **123 requirements** (0 errors, 0 warnings) across all new APIs. Every new function is traced via source annotations, tested with MC/DC witnesses, and covered by the structure-aware fuzzer.

##### Config struct — opt-in lenient parsing ([#​160](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/160), [#​115](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/115))

```go
var Lenient = jsonparser.Config{AllowSingleQuotes: true, AllowUnknownEscapes: true}
Lenient.Get(data, "key")  // parses {'key':'value'} and unknown escapes
```

- **`AllowSingleQuotes`** — accept `'key':'value'` alongside `"key":"value"` (JavaScript/Python-style). The same escape rules apply inside single-quoted strings.
- **`AllowUnknownEscapes`** — pass through unknown escape sequences (`` \` ``, `\x`) literally instead of erroring.
- The default Config is strict (RFC 8259 only). Package-level functions are unchanged.
- Config methods mirror the full API: `Get`, `GetString`, `Set`, `Delete`, `ArrayEach`, `ObjectEach`.

##### Streaming ReaderParser ([#​132](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/132), [#​257](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/257))

```go
rp := jsonparser.NewReaderParser(file)  // any io.Reader
rp.Get("users", "[0]", "name")          // path-based access from a stream
```

- Path-based access to JSON data from an `io.Reader` — **no need to load the entire document into memory**.
- Buffers data incrementally in 64KB chunks; memory is bounded by the largest value, not the document size.
- Enables parsing **10GB+ JSON files** without OOM.
- Methods: `Get`, `GetString`, `ArrayEach`.

##### Name aliases ([#​66](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/66))

Canonical `EachXxx` pattern added alongside existing `XxxEach` names:

| New (canonical)     | Old (kept for compat) |
| ------------------- | --------------------- |
| `EachArray`         | `ArrayEach`           |
| `EachObject`        | `ObjectEach`          |
| `EachArrayErr`      | `ArrayEachErr`        |
| `EachArrayWildcard` | `ArrayEachWildcard`   |

`EachKey`, `EachKeyErr`, `EachKeyWildcard` already matched the pattern. All old names remain functional.

##### Proof

- 2 new SYS-REQs: 115 (Config/lenient parsing), 116 (streaming ReaderParser)
- **123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 279/279 functions traced**

***

### [`v1.4.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v140--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.3.1...v1.4.0)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance

v1.4.0 adds 9 new backward-compatible APIs, each traced to a formal requirement and verified with MC/DC coverage. **121 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings.**

##### New APIs

**Iteration with error/break control** — resolves [#​53](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/53), [#​129](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/129), [#​176](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/176), [#​230](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/230), [#​255](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/255), [#​262](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/262)

- `ArrayEachErr` — callback returns `error` to stop early (`io.EOF` = graceful stop)
- `EachKeyErr` — same pattern for EachKey

**Safe string handling** — resolves [#​144](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/144), [#​158](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/158), [#​218](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/218), [#​270](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/270)

- `Escape(s string) []byte` — RFC 8259 string escaping (inverse of `Unescape`)
- `SetString(data, val, keys...)` — Set with auto-quoted value

**Container accessors** — resolves [#​175](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/175), [#​261](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/261), [#​271](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/271)

- `GetArrayLen` / `GetObjectLen` — count elements without a callback
- `GetUint64` — uint64 variant of `GetInt`

**Delete found signal** — resolves [#​229](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/229)

- `DeleteFound(data, keys...) ([]byte, bool)` — returns whether the key was found

**Wildcard paths** — resolves [#​112](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/112)

- `EachKeyWildcard`, `ArrayEachWildcard`, `SetWildcard` — `[*]` path component

**JSONPath compiled paths** — resolves [#​234](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/234), [#​251](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/251)

- `ParsePath("$.users[0].name")` → `[]string` path
- `CompilePath` + `CompiledPath` — pre-compile and reuse with Get/Set/Delete

##### Fixes

- EachKey no longer panics with >64 key components ([#​56](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/56))
- Set pre-allocates output buffer, reducing allocations from 6 to 1 ([#​107](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/107))

##### Proof

- 3 new SYS-REQs: 112 (container length), 113 (wildcard paths), 114 (compiled paths)
- **121 requirements, 384 MC/DC witness rows, 0 uncovered**

***

### [`v1.3.1`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v131--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.3.0...v1.3.1)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance

v1.3.1 fixes 3 bugs that escaped the initial proof review, with new proof gates to prevent recurrence.

##### Bug fixes

- **Fix Set/Delete input-buffer aliasing** ([#​209](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/209), [#​141](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/141)) — `Set` and `Delete` no longer corrupt the caller's input `[]byte` when the slice has spare capacity. All mutation paths now allocate a fresh buffer.
- **Fix EachKey array-index inconsistency** ([#​232](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/232)) — `EachKey` now descends into terminal array-index paths consistently with `Get`.
- **Fix benchmark measuring ffjson, not encoding/json** ([#​126](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/126)) — benchmark payload types stripped of generated methods.

##### Proof strengthening

| Bug                                                                                                                        | Proof gap                                                 | New gate                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [#​209](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/209)/[#​141](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/141) Set aliasing | No obligation said "Set must not mutate the input buffer" | New obligation `no_input_mutation` + `assertInputUnchanged` gate |
| [#​232](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/232) EachKey ≠ Get                                                       | No cross-API consistency obligation                       | New obligation `api_consistency` + differential gate             |
| [#​126](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/126) benchmark ffjson                                                    | Proof didn't cover benchmarks                             | Benchmark honesty lint                                           |

***

### [`v1.3.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v130--2026-07-27)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.2.0...v1.3.0)

##### Formally verified by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com)

jsonparser v1.3.0 is the **first Go library proven to L3 assurance** by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com), a git-native requirements-engineering and formal-verification platform. The entire codebase is now covered by:

- **118 formal requirements** (7 stakeholder + 111 system-level), each traced to code via source annotations and verified with FRETish formalization.
- **100% Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC)** — both code-level (every decision/condition branch exercised) and requirement-side (377/377 truth-table rows witnessed).
- **A custom structure-aware JSON fuzzer** ([github.com/probelabs/json-fuzz](https://redirect.github.com/probelabs/json-fuzz)) generating grammar-valid mutations at 250k inputs/sec, plus path-mutation and `encoding/json` differential harnesses.
- **L3 strict audit posture**: 0 errors, 0 warnings, all checks enabled.

The proof review found and fixed **7 real bugs** that years of community use, OSS-Fuzz, and standard fuzzing had missed. [Read the root-cause analysis →](docs/proof-gap-root-cause.md)

jsonparser serves as the **reference case study** for ReqProof — [learn more at reqproof.com](https://reqproof.com).

##### Security / bug fixes

- **Fix Delete panic on malformed input with leading comma** (OSS-Fuzz [`4649128`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/commit/4649128545288192))
  `Delete` panicked with `index out of range [-1]` on inputs like `,{"test":1{}`.
  The `data[prevTok]` dereference is now guarded.

- **Fix empty-string key-component panics** (8 sites)
  `Get`, `GetString`, `GetInt`, `GetFloat`, `GetBoolean`, `GetUnsafeString`, `Set`,
  `Delete`, `EachKey` panicked with `index out of range [0]` when a key path contained
  an empty string (`""`). All 8 unguarded `keys[i][0]` dereference sites are now guarded
  with `len(...) > 0`. Found by the structure-aware hazard sweep.
  Reported by [@​c-tonneslan](https://redirect.github.com/c-tonneslan) ([#​284](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/284)).

- **Fix Set data loss on scalar arrays** ([#​267](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/267))
  `Set` on an array-index path beyond the current length silently overwrote the array
  instead of appending. `Set({"a":[1,2,3]}, 99, "a", "[9]")` now returns `{"a":[1,2,3,99]}`
  instead of `{"a":[99]}`. Reported by [@​Solaris-star](https://redirect.github.com/Solaris-star) ([#​286](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/286)).

- **Fix Set malformed-JSON output on cross-type paths**
  `Set` with an array-index path component under an object parent (e.g. `Set({}, 9, "[5]")`)
  produced invalid JSON (`{[9]}`). Set now auto-coerces the container type to match the
  path, always producing valid JSON output.

- **Fix Delete trailing-comma malformation**
  `Delete` left a dangling trailing comma in the output when the deleted element was
  followed by JSON whitespace (space/tab/LF/CR) and a comma. Found by the structure-aware
  path-mutation fuzzer.

- **Fix ArrayEach spurious callback on non-array root**
  `ArrayEach` on a non-array root value (e.g. `ArrayEach({"a":1}, cb)`) invoked the
  callback with a spurious element before returning an error. The callback is no longer
  invoked; a clean error is returned immediately.

- **Fix lone-Unicode-surrogate mishandling in Unescape**
  `ParseString` on a string containing a lone high surrogate (e.g. `\uDB29` without a
  following low surrogate) synthesized a bogus non-BMP code point from the following
  literal bytes. Now substitutes U+FFFD (matching `encoding/json` behavior).

##### Performance

- **parseInt fast-path for short numbers** — 22–37% faster on typical 1–10 digit integers.
  Numbers with ≤18 digits use direct int64 accumulation, bypassing the overflow-checked
  uint64 slow path. Contributed by [@​trevorprater](https://redirect.github.com/trevorprater) ([#​285](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/285)).

- **stringEnd SIMD fast path** — 12× faster on no-escape strings, 4.5× faster end-to-end
  on `Get` for string values. Uses `bytes.IndexByte` for the common case (no `\` before
  the closing `"`).

##### Acknowledgments

- [@​c-tonneslan](https://redirect.github.com/c-tonneslan) ([#​284](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/284)) — reported the empty-string key-component panic
- [@​Solaris-star](https://redirect.github.com/Solaris-star) ([#​286](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/286)) — reported the Set array-index data-loss bug ([#​267](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/267))
- [@​trevorprater](https://redirect.github.com/trevorprater) ([#​285](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/285)) — contributed the parseInt performance optimization
- OSS-Fuzz (issue [`4649128`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/commit/4649128545288192)) — the original Delete leading-comma panic
- The [probelabs/json-fuzz](https://redirect.github.com/probelabs/json-fuzz) structure-aware fuzzer

items.title: Scale the Bengali tokenizer to a literary-weighted 64k model, beating IndicBERTv2 everywhere
items.body:
## Summary

- Real literary-weighted training corpus (Wikisource, AI4Bharat Sangraha, Wikipedia, XL-Sum news) replaces the Wikipedia-only v0.1 corpus, with OCR-noise filtering and disjoint per-register held-out reservation.
- Vocab-size ablation (32k/48k/64k) showed fertility recovering monotonically with vocab size; 64k is the smallest size that beats IndicBERTv2 on fertility, STRR, **and** conjunct fragmentation across every held-out register tested (Wikipedia, literary/formal, general web, news). New official artifact: `artifacts/bn-bpe-64k`.
- Two real correctness fixes grounded in direct `unicodedata` verification: Bengali's danda/double-danda punctuation was missing from the guaranteed-coverage set (it's a shared Devanagari-block codepoint, not Bengali-block); `ড়/ঢ়/য়` now re-compose to their single dedicated codepoint after NFC (a minor efficiency fix — NFC already unified both spellings, just onto the decomposed form, contrary to what the old docstring claimed).
- `scripts/compare.py`'s own fragmentation counter for our tokenizer had two real measurement bugs (a Metaspace leading-space off-by-one, and `encode_tokens()` returning the literal string `"<unk>"` for out-of-coverage foreign-script text), both caught by a hard assertion added specifically to catch this class of mistake. Full three-version account in `docs/known-issues.md` point 8.
- New `docs/bengali-script-reference.md`: full Bengali Unicode block inventory and grapheme-cluster rules, verified against Python's own Unicode database rather than recalled from memory — including two mistakes made and corrected in the open.
- README, paper (arXiv preprint source), website, and both CHANGELOGs updated with the verified numbers; Hugging Face model card/tokenizer files staged (not yet pushed to the live Hub repo — that's a separate step).

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/` — 15/15 passing
- [x] Round-trip and fragmentation numbers regenerated end-to-end against the actual shipped `artifacts/bn-bpe-64k` artifact (not just the training-time staging copy), with an assertion guarding the measurement itself
- [x] Reproduce commands in README/benchmarks/paper actually match what's shipped in `artifacts/`
- [x] Reviewer: skim `docs/known-issues.md` for anything that reads as overclaiming — this branch deliberately keeps the mistakes made along the way, not just the final numbers

items.title: release: v2.3.1 "Plumb Line" — measurement apparatus, and ten measured rejections
items.body:
Closes nothing; opens the v2.3.x performance line.

v2.3.1 builds the measurement apparatus and then uses it. The core hot-path
campaign originally planned as a separate v2.3.2 "Grain" ran to completion,
**measured ten items and rejected all ten**, and so had no shippable content of
its own — it is folded in here, because these results are the answer this
tooling existed to produce. The "Grain" name moves to the frontend work.

**No emulation-core changes.** AccuracyCoin holds at exactly 141/141 and nestest
is 0-diff, verified after every experimental probe was reverted rather than
merely by construction — this branch did land and remove real edits.

## Why the tooling came first

Two failures motivated it, both from the immediately preceding release:

1. **v2.3.0 P1 measured `+2%` on a contended host and `−5.13%` re-measured
   quiet** — the same commit, opposite sign. Nothing in the tooling noticed the
   host.
2. **The profile the campaign was scoped from does not contain the APU.**
   `perf report` shows zero `rustynes_apu::` symbols at any percent limit,
   because fat LTO inlines the APU wholesale into `cpu_clock`. The working split
   "PPU ~53%, CPU+bus ~39%" silently folded ~19% of the frame into the wrong
   bucket.

## What the tooling found

| tool | what it revealed |
| --- | --- |
| `frame_probe` | criterion's own rayon/`exp`/sort work was ~17% of every profile |
| `frame_breakdown.sh` | **APU is 18.7% of frame**, invisible in the symbol view (`--inline` does not recover it) |
| `ab_check.sh` A/B/A control | the reference drifts up to −1.17% from run *position alone* |

Corrected split: **PPU 52.1% / APU 18.7% / CPU 10.1% / coupling 9.9% /
std-inlined 6.7% / mappers 2.5%.** The CPU proper is about a third of what the
symbol profile implied.

## Ten items, ten rejections, six mechanisms

| mechanism | items |
| --- | --- |
| LLVM already performs the transformation | G3 sink dead derivations |
| the premise is factually false | G2 `repr(Rust)` ignores source order; G7 already inlined |
| real work, absorbed off the critical path | G4 store buffer; G5 predicted branches; G6 recompute |
| the elision is real but buys nothing | G8 bounds checks |
| the target is too small | G9 (0.09% of frame) |
| forbidden by the ownership model | G10 borrow checker |

The diversity is the point: this is not one bad assumption repeated. **The
per-dot loop has no incidental overhead left to reclaim** — its ~3.78 ms is work
the accuracy model requires. That corroborates the existing record, where
`emit_pixel` bounds-check elision and the SIMD blitter both measured *slower*.

## Two near-misses worth reading

- **G2** produced a textbook **−1.84%…−2.75% at p = 0.00 on all four
  workloads** — from an order-bias artifact. It measured as exactly zero on
  re-run. This is what prompted the A/B/A control.
- **G6** measured **−0.51% at p = 0.00 on `nestest_fast`, a shipped
  configuration**, with a clean control on that workload. Re-run: **+0.01%
  (p = 0.96)**. Under the relaxed sub-3% adoption bar, run 1 alone was an adopt.

Both were caught only by the mandatory second run. Method notes are recorded in
`docs/performance.md` alongside the numbers.

## Also here

- The relative frame-time gate declines to emit a verdict on a contended host.
- The BOLT probe no longer trusts `apt-get install bolt` — on Ubuntu that package
  is the **Thunderbolt 3 device manager**, so the stage failed on the tool it had
  just "confirmed" instead of skipping. (BOLT itself remains unmeasured; a
  follow-up fix for its runtime library is on the Grain branch.)

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --features test-roms` green; AccuracyCoin **141/141**,
  `visual_regression` 9/9.
- Workspace clippy clean at `-D warnings`; `cargo fmt --all --check` clean.
- `bash -n` + `shellcheck` clean on all touched scripts.

items.title: test(transpiler): benchmark measured circuits, fix measurement-dropping converters, refresh floors
items.body:
Stacked on #1312 (first two commits are that branch; review the last two commits). Together with #1312 this completes the weights/floors program from #1307.

## What changed since the first push

The original version routed *around* measurement-dropping conversions with reduced weights. The final commit fixes the converters themselves, so measurements now survive **every** conversion path and the compensating weights are gone:

- **`cirq_to_braket`** converted `MeasurementGate`s to `[]`. It now emits Braket `Measure` instructions (with `X` for `invert_mask` bits). Mid-circuit measurement raises `ProgramConversionError` — Braket cannot represent it, and Braket's own "cannot apply instruction to measured qubits" check is what enforces it.
- **`pytket_to_braket`** re-appends the measurements pytket's `tk_to_braket` silently discards, in classical-bit order via the qubit mapping `tk_to_braket` returns. Mid-circuit measurement raises rather than silently becoming terminal. Weight 0.95 removed → 1.0.
- **`braket_to_cirq`** collected each Braket measure as a keyless `M('')`, which downstream QASM/Quil exports collapse into `BIT[1]`. Braket measures are always terminal, so they now merge into one keyed `MeasurementGate`. Weight 0.99 (unexplained since #880) removed → 1.0.
- **`cirq_to_pyquil`** declared one `BIT[1]` register per measurement key (`c_0`, `c_1`, ... from QASM-derived circuits) — the fragmented form QCS rejects ("Misplaced or illegal instruction in ProtoQuil program", 23 production jobs). A pre-pass now merges *terminal* measurements into one keyed gate, producing a single `DECLARE <name> BIT[n]`. Genuinely mid-circuit keys are left alone, so the vendored `QuilOutput` multi-key semantics (and its pinned test) are untouched.
- **`cudaq_to_qasm2`** (found by the new suite): `cudaq.translate` reports failure by *returning the string* `"{translation failed}"` — the transpiler passed it along as a successful conversion. It now raises so `transpile()` falls back to the next path.

`KNOWN_MEASUREMENT_FAILURES` is now **empty** — no follow-up issue needed. The set and its exactness contract stay: a pair joining it is a regression CI will name.

## Strategy (proposed as doctrine)

- **Floors are regression tripwires, not routing inputs**: set to measured-cold minus ~2 points (the #1226 pattern), refreshed when measured accuracy moves. Cold = isolated process, because xdist makes warm/cold a scheduling lottery.
- **Weights are routing preferences**: structural behavior (measurements, registers, placement) outranks gate fidelity — but the first choice is to *fix the converter*, and only weight-route around what can't be fixed. Any weight change must pass both the gate-coverage and measurement suites. No sub-1.0 values without a comment saying why.
- **`KNOWN_MEASUREMENT_FAILURES` is exact**: a pair leaving it (fix) or joining it (regression) both fail CI.

The one deliberately low weight left: `cirq_to_pyquil` keeps 0.74 (below the e^-0.25 ≈ 0.7788 break-even) on pure gate-fidelity grounds — routing through qasm2 measures ~0.95 vs ~0.88 direct. The comment now records that rationale instead of the fixed fragmentation.

## Numbers

Floors raised (measured cold in a CI-matched env — qiskit 2.3.0, pytket 2.18.1, numpy 2.4.6; identical results under the older local versions):

| pair | floor was | measured | floor now |
|---|---|---|---|
| cirq → pyquil | 0.74 | 0.875 | 0.85 |
| pyquil → braket | 0.77 | 0.852 | 0.83 |
| pyquil → cirq/pytket/qiskit | 0.77 | 0.889 | 0.86 |
| braket → pyquil | 0.84 | 0.974 | 0.95 |

`qiskit_to_qasm2` 0.999 → 1.0 (no benchmark basis; routes move to qasm2 on ties, gate coverage stays 1.0, measured circuits survive).

Measurement sweep: **56 passed, 8 skipped, 0 known failures** — including `cirq → braket` and `pytket → braket`, which lose measurements on `main`. Full `tests/transpiler` + `tests/programs`: 1386 passed; remaining failures are pre-existing on `main` in this env (`test_cirq_pytket_direct_conversions`, plus cudaq-translate tests broken on macOS arm64 — CI's Linux cudaq is unaffected).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

  * Preserved measurement operations when converting circuits between supported quantum frameworks.
  * Improved handling of terminal measurements, measured-qubit ordering, and inversion masks.
  * Added clearer conversion errors for unsupported mid-circuit measurements and invalid CUDA-Q translations.
  * Prevented gates after measurements from being silently accepted where unsupported.

* **Improvements**
  * Improved conversion accuracy and routing decisions through updated benchmarks and coverage validation.
  * Added broader measurement-conversion testing across supported program formats.

items.title: Benchmark RegexSearchEngine search-vs-mutate and price the #920 consistency fix
items.body:
## Summary

Adds `regex_search_benchmark` and reports what #920's `Search` change actually
costs. That change made `Search` point-in-time consistent by retrying a query a
mutation lands under, with a fully-locked pass as the fallback — a real cost
that nothing measured at the time.

## What it measures

Three quantities that pull against each other:

1. **Uncontended search** — the tax on every query that never races. Should be
   ~free: one relaxed atomic load and a compare.
2. **Contended search** — retry amplification. Each retry repeats the candidate
   scan *and* the regex pass.
3. **Mutate throughput** — the #680 regression guard. #680 moved the regex pass
   out of the lock because 3 tight-loop searchers vs 8 writers hung the parallel
   test; the locked fallback puts it back, rarely. Defaults reproduce that shape.

It also reports **mean entries per listing**, so a throughput win that silently
drops entries cannot read as a win.

## Results (3 s per phase, `iowarp/deps-cpu`)

**5000-entry directory — worst case**

| | before #920 | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| search, uncontended | 409 ops/s | 432 ops/s | no measurable cost |
| search, contended | 1078 ops/s | 310 ops/s | **−71%** |
| mutate | 56,472 ops/s | 44,402 ops/s | −21% |
| **entries/listing** | **4853 / 5000** | **5000 / 5000** | the bug, quantified |

**100-entry directory — realistic readdir**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| search, contended | 43,569 ops/s (67 µs) | 17,146 ops/s (174 µs) |
| mutate | 58,323 ops/s | 68,350 ops/s |
| entries/listing | 97.4 / 100 | 100 / 100 |

The pre-#920 numbers were fast because the results were **wrong** — under rename
churn it dropped ~147 of 5000 entries from every listing. At realistic directory
sizes the correctness costs ~107 µs per listing under heavy concurrent rename,
and writers actually got faster.

## The `kOptimisticAttempts` knob

Not obvious from the code, so worth recording:

| attempts | search | mutate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 613 ops/s | 25,452 ops/s |
| **3 (shipped)** | 310 ops/s | 44,402 ops/s |

Fewer attempts reach the locked fallback sooner: better for readers, **43% worse
for writers**. Since #680 was specifically a writer-starvation bug, 3 is the
safer setting — now backed by measurement rather than judgement.

## Known limitation, not addressed here

Under sustained churn the optimistic path rarely wins: with mutations at ~70k/s,
nearly every search sees a version bump and falls through to the locked pass. The
counter is global, so churn on keys that *cannot* affect a query still
invalidates it. Making the version check finer-grained (per prefix/bucket) is the
real fix for the 5000-entry contended case; this PR only measures the problem.

## Test plan

- [x] Builds in `iowarp/deps-cpu`
- [x] A/B run against `512e8740^` (pre-fix) and current `dev`
- [x] Benchmark only — no product code touched

## Breaking changes

None. New benchmark target; nothing else changes.

items.title: v0.6: cross-vendor + short-plan corpus, with measurement-bug correction
items.body:
## Summary

Ships v0.6 of the benchmark: Anthropic Claude added (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7), a new short-plan corpus (5 scenarios, 1–4 week plans), a re-run multi-turn protocol, and **the correction of a measurement bug** that had produced a false "0/180 violations" headline.

Frozen tag: `v0.6.0`. Full write-up: `docs/V0_6_RESULTS.md`.

## ⚠️ Read first: why ~500 result files changed

A Lane B plan-walker (`extractFromWplJson`) was reading the wrong path in the compiled WPL JSON after the wpl-ai compiler changed shape — it walked `phases[].weeks[].days[].{warmup,main,cooldown}.items[]` instead of the real `plan.phases[].weeks[].days[].blocks[].activities[]`. It silently returned an empty plan for every Lane B trial, so the scorer saw nothing and reported zero violations. The retracted `v0.6.0-anthropic` snapshot's "0/180" was "the extractor saw nothing," not "the contract caught everything."

The walker is fixed and **every Lane B result was re-derived from stored model output — no new API calls.** The large result-file diff is mechanical re-derivation, not hand edits. The substantive review surface is ~30 files (see below).

## Four bugs found and fixed
1. **Lane B JSON walker** (`e02edb2`) — the "0/180" artifact above.
2. **Short-plan scorer rules** (`93e9deb`) — rest-day counting, progression cap, on-ramp intensity ratio, peaking-taper comparison.
3. **Multi-turn final-turn semantics** (`ef78760` + `d92f123`) — the summary-turn prompt forced prose, which Lane B's DSL-only system prompt correctly refused; the walker read that as a compile failure. Fixed via latest-valid-turn semantics + a re-emission prompt.
4. **Markdown-fence stripping** (`d92f123`) — small models wrap DSL in ``` blocks; wpl-ai treated them as parse errors.

Full disclosure: `docs/V0_6_RESULTS.md` → "The four corrected bugs."

## Corrected findings
- The WPL contract reduces unsafe-trial rate **3–5×** across every corpus and both phases (single + multi-turn) — not to zero.
- Lane A safety **degrades with model capability**: the two flagships (Opus 4.7, gpt-5) are the worst raw performers; the cheapest (Haiku, gpt-4.1) are safest. (Lane A was never touched by the bug — it scores prose, not compiled JSON.)
- The **schema validator**, not the compile gate, is the served-rate ceiling; failures concentrate at the activity block.
- **DSL→compile** does real schema-conformance work direct JSON emission can't substitute for (native-JSON probes).
- The **short-plan corpus** surfaces structural failures (rest days, progression, on-ramp) the raw prose lane is blind to; multi-turn conversations drive structural drift the contract surfaces but doesn't yet prevent (v0.7 work).

## Substantive review surface (~30 files)
- `src/scoring/short-plan.ts` — new short-plan scorer (5 rule families)
- `src/lanes/lane-b.ts` — the walker fix + fence stripping
- `src/lanes/lane-a.ts`, `src/runner.ts`, `src/lib/types.ts` — short-plan wiring + types
- `src/models/anthropic.ts`, `src/lib/pricing.ts` — Anthropic adapter (Opus temperature handling)
- `src/scripts/rescore-*.ts` — offline re-derivation tooling (how the correction was produced for \$0)
- `scenarios/scenarios.yaml` — +5 short-plan scenarios, multi-turn final-turn change
- `test/short-plan.test.ts`, `test/anthropic-adapter.test.ts` — new tests
- `docs/V0_6_RESULTS.md`, `README.md` — corrected write-ups

## Verification
- `npm run typecheck` — clean
- `npm test` — 125/125 pass
- 560 trials, ~\$170 total inference; every number reproducible from committed output for \$0

## Note
`v0.6.0-anthropic` is retained for historical traceability but **should not be cited** — it predates the correction.

## Summary

Implements v0.2 PR-8 per `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-28-v0-2-pr8-release-profile-pycctoml-nbody.md` and the design spec's §1 nbody contract:

- `pycc.toml` parsing + `pycc init` scaffolding (D-092)
- `--release` CLI flag wired to LLVM's `default<O3>` pass pipeline via inkwell's `Module::run_passes` (D-092), and to a release-built `pycc_rt` static library instead of always linking the debug build (D-090)
- `tests/fixtures/nbody.py`: hand-adapted, fully-unrolled, scalar-only 5-body simulation using only pycc's shipped v0.1 grammar (D-092), iteration count raised to 525000 to amortize the paired benchmark's fixed per-process overhead (D-091)
- `tests/nbody_bench.rs`: same-machine paired median-of-5 comparison, `--release` pycc vs. pinned CPython 3.14.6, gated at ratio ≥ 20
- CI: release-profile `pycc_rt` build step on `build-test-coverage` and all 5 Tier-1 `native-build-test` legs, staged/activated through the two-phase CI-workflow-digest trust boundary (D-090, PR #187 merged as the stage step)

## Known-red test — this PR intentionally opens with `nbody_bench` failing

`tests/nbody_bench.rs` currently measures **~18.0–18.24x** on this one macOS development machine, short of the design spec's `≥ 20x` gate (see D-091). This is an honest measurement failure, not a bug: the harness, the `--release`/`pycc_rt` fix, the iteration-count amortization, and the CI wiring are all correct and verified — the ratio itself is simply short of the gate on this one data point.

**This PR exists partly to collect real numbers, not just to land green.** Process overhead and libm/codegen throughput vary by platform (especially Windows vs. Linux vs. macOS), so the actual gate-value decision — whether 20x needs revising, whether more optimization work is warranted, or whether the current number already clears the bar elsewhere — is deliberately deferred until `nbody_bench`'s ratio is observed on all 5 Tier-1 CI legs, not guessed from one machine. Expect `ci-gate` to run red on this PR's first CI pass; that is the point of opening it now.

items.title: fix(test): stop gogitstore heap-benchmark tests flaking under CI load
items.body:
## Summary
- Fixes recurring CI flakes in `session/unfinished/gogitstore` for `TestMmapIndex_HeapAllocation_LowerThanCopyBased` and `TestSharedIndex_SecondAndLaterWorktreesCostLessThanFirst` — root cause is a measurement-methodology bug (process-wide `TotalAlloc`, single-sample strict comparisons), not a code regression.
- `TestConcurrentReadsAcrossWorktrees_NoDataRace` was investigated separately and confirmed to be a legitimate `-race` correctness test, unrelated to the heap-measurement issue — left unchanged.

## Context
Three tests in this package were flaking under CI load (4+ concurrent PR runs). The two heap-allocation tests measure real memory via `runtime.ReadMemStats()` and assert a relative ordering between two arms (mmap loader vs copy-based loader; first worktree open vs later worktree opens). One of them read `TotalAlloc`, a process-wide **monotonic** counter — any concurrent allocation in the same test binary (GC background workers, the `mmapwatch.go` pack-watch goroutine `ensureIndex` starts for `useMmap=true`, scheduler jitter under a loaded runner) permanently inflates the delta and can flip a close comparison. Re-running the exact same failing CI jobs with zero code changes passed cleanly, confirming this as a measurement flaw rather than an implementation regression.

Investigated moving these to the repo's existing benchmark CI tiers (`Go Benchmarks Tier 1/2`) first — not clean: those tiers run `go test -bench=. -run='^$'`, i.e. true `Benchmark*` functions compared against a stored baseline via `benchstat`, an entirely different comparison model (baseline-vs-current across runs) than what these tests do (a live two-arm comparison within a single run), and the tests entangle functional assertions (`IndexBuildCount`, mmap handle nil-checks) with the performance comparison. Splitting that apart was a bigger, riskier change than warranted for this fix — hardened the measurement in place instead.

## Changes
- **`session/unfinished/gogitstore/gogitstore_test.go`**: expanded `heapAllocNow()`'s doc comment to explain why it deliberately reads `HeapAlloc` (live, GC'd) rather than `TotalAlloc` (monotonic); added a `median()` helper; relaxed `TestSharedIndex_SecondAndLaterWorktreesCostLessThanFirst`'s strict `avgLater >= first` check to a documented 50%-of-first tolerance ceiling (real observed margin is ~80x, so this stays tight against actual regressions).
- **`session/unfinished/gogitstore/mmap_stage2_test.go`**: rewrote `TestMmapIndex_HeapAllocation_LowerThanCopyBased` to reuse `heapAllocNow()`/`deltaOrZero()` instead of ad hoc `TotalAlloc` deltas, take the median of 5 samples per arm, and compare against a tolerance ceiling instead of a strict `<`. The ceiling (90%) is calibrated against **both** non-`-race` (~26% ratio) and `-race` (~82% ratio, structurally different — not noise — due to race-detector bookkeeping adding proportionally more fixed cost to the mmap path's locking/goroutine machinery) since CI's `Test` job always runs `go test -race`.
- **Tests**: no new test files — hardened the existing three tests' methodology in place.

## Impact
- **Scope**: `session/unfinished/gogitstore` test files only. No production code changed.
- **Breaking Changes**: none.
- **Performance**: none — this only changes how tests measure and assert, not runtime behavior.
- **Dependencies**: none.

## Testing
- [x] `go test ./session/unfinished/gogitstore/... -run 'TestMmapIndex_HeapAllocation_LowerThanCopyBased|TestSharedIndex_SecondAndLaterWorktreesCostLessThanFirst|TestConcurrentReadsAcrossWorktrees_NoDataRace' -race -count=10` — 30/30 passing
- [x] Full `go test ./session/unfinished/gogitstore/... -race` (untargeted) — passing
- [x] `gofmt -l` and `golangci-lint run` clean on both changed files

## Reviewer Notes
- **Focus areas**: the tolerance ratios (90% for mmap-vs-copy, 50% for later-vs-first-worktree) are the main judgment call — sized with real margin against both `-race` and non-`-race` observed numbers, documented inline with the rationale.
- **Known limitations**: these are still process-wide heap measurements (not goroutine-scoped), so some theoretical flake risk remains under extreme load; the tolerance margins and median sampling are a pragmatic mitigation, not a hard guarantee.
- **Follow-up tasks**: none identified — `TestConcurrentReadsAcrossWorktrees_NoDataRace` needed no changes.

items.title: eval: measure the reach claim — and falsify it
items.body: `grip-search`'s pitch rested on **reach**: that a real browser retrieves content a static-fetch vendor cannot see, because that content is rendered by JavaScript. Cost and latency were measured. Reach was the claim justifying being 3–5x slower, and it had never been tested. **It does not hold.** ## Method Both arms fetch the **same URL**, so only the fetch mechanism varies — nothing about ranking, discovery or pricing confounds it. - **browser** — grip, real Chrome, `page.read()` - **static** — plain HTTP GET, tags stripped, entities decoded The marker is picked by a **fixed rule** — the first 12 words of the longest content block the browser found — so it cannot be chosen to flatter. 33 URLs across four categories, deliberately including cases the browser should lose. ## Result | category | n | browser | static | gap | |---|---|---|---|---| | static | 12 | 11 | 11 | **0** | | spa | 9 | 7 | 7 | **0** | | hybrid | 8 | 5 | 5 | **0** | | protected | 4 | 0 | 0 | **0** | | **total** | **33** | **23** | **23** | **0** | Zero gap, **including SPAs**. ## Why it failed Modern documentation sites server-render **because they need SEO**. react.dev, vuejs.org, angular.dev, svelte.dev, tanstack.com, nextjs.org — all ship content in the initial payload. The premise confused *"built as an SPA"* with *"content only exists after JS runs"*. For anything wanting Google traffic, the second is commercially impossible. Where static fetch fails, it fails on **blocking**, not rendering — and blocking beats the browser too. All four protected pages defeated both arms. A headless browser is not a way around Cloudflare. ## The one measured advantage On pages where both succeeded, static fetch returns a **median 1.4x the characters** for the same substance — the excess being nav, footers and script residue. That reframes the README's 19x token figure: | baseline | grip is | relevant when | |---|---|---| | raw HTML | ~19x smaller | you'd otherwise put HTML in the prompt | | tag-stripped text | **~1.4x smaller** | comparing against a retrieval vendor | Both true. The second is the honest comparison against Tavily, because no retrieval vendor sends raw HTML to a model. ## Two measurement bugs, both of which had inflated the browser's score 1. **Whitespace** — tag-stripping inserts a space at every tag boundary, so `foobar` reads as `foo bar` statically and `foobar` through innerText. Scored 10 false browser wins. 2. **HTML entities** — `->` is `->`; the normaliser folded the stray `gt` into the text as letters, breaking matches on any page containing code. Scored 8 more. Gap went 10 → 8 → 1 → 0. The last "win" was a dead URL where the browser read a 404 page and the static arm correctly discarded the error. Recorded in the writeup, because a benchmark that has never been wrong has probably never been checked. ## What this means The product's central claim, as written, does not survive measurement. Three honest positions remain, none of them "better reach": 1. **Structure and citations** — real, demonstrable, but a *quality* claim 2. **Knowing when a fetch failed** — untested, worth its own experiment 3. **Interaction-to-reveal** (ticket 09) — the **only surviving reach hypothesis**, and unbuilt Ticket 09 was deferred on the reasoning "prove reach before extending it". That reasoning holds; the conclusion inverts. Rendered-DOM reach is disproven, so interaction-to-reveal is no longer optional — it is the entire hypothesis. ## Also in this PR **CI was only running `tests/unit/`.** 65 of 175 tests — every integration and gripsearch test — never executed there. Now added. They are offline (local `http.server` fixtures) but need a Chrome binary, which `ubuntu-latest` ships. Watching this PR's check to confirm. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_014MuGgwDCPSCf7VoW6yqbZ4

items.title: feat: persist and grade research decision snapshots
items.body:
Closes the second half of the research loop. #150 made the live path **emit** the canonical `Prediction` contract; nothing stored or judged it. This persists each day's snapshot and grades it into `ExecutableOutcome` records once horizons elapse.

## Persistence — `lib/research/store.js`

Two **separate** Blob prefixes:

```
research/decisions/<date>.json   immutable DecisionSnapshot (write-once)
research/outcomes/<date>.json    grader-owned OutcomeBatch
```

The split is structural, not conventional. The contract requires that ingestion never overwrite grading and grading never mutate a prediction — two prefixes with two writers make that **impossible to violate by accident**. A grader bug can corrupt outcomes but can never rewrite the decision being judged.

Decisions are **write-once**: `op=today` runs many times a day, and without the guard the evening call would silently replace the morning's record. A prediction that can be rewritten after the fact is not evidence.

## Grading — `lib/research/grade.js`

Four rules, all tested:

1. **Never grade early.** An unelapsed horizon returns `pending` with a reason, never a smaller number. Grading a 63-session prediction at day 5 is how a loser becomes a "winner".
2. **Entry is a real fill** — next session open, never the decision close. An unfillable name is *recorded* as `unfilled` with its reason; dropping such names would be survivorship bias inside the grader.
3. **Rejected candidates are graded too.** The outcome answers *what the market did*; the prediction's `state` answers *whether we selected it*. Skipping rejects would rebuild the selection-bias trap one layer down.
4. **Costs are side-aware** — spread plus short borrow over the real holding period, so a short is never scored as if borrow were free.

## Route — `op=researchgrade`

Bounded to 3 days / 120 tickers per invocation to fit the 60s function budget; a partial pass is fine because the next run continues. Idempotent — re-grading recomputes from immutable inputs, so retries are always safe.

## Two measurement bugs the tests caught

Neither was visible by reading the code, and both would have quietly biased **every** result this loop ever produced.

**Slippage was double-charged.** `execution-policy`'s default policy (`NEXT_OPEN_PLUS_SLIPPAGE`) bakes entry slippage into the fill *price*, while `costs.js` separately charges `2 × (halfSpread + slippage)`. Using both charges the entry leg twice and makes every strategy look worse than it is. Now fills at the unslipped `NEXT_OPEN` and lets `costs.js` be the sole friction model — which also keeps a research outcome directly comparable to a Scoreboard net return.

**Benchmark entry timing was misaligned.** The position enters at the fill session's **open**, but the benchmark was measured close-to-close — a different window, biasing every residual by one bar's open-to-close move. Both legs now run `open(entry) → close(exit)`.

The failing assertion was *"residual should be ~ −costs when the name IS the benchmark"*: **−0.243 vs −0.16**. Both fixes are pinned by regression tests, including an exact-equality check that fails on any reintroduced drift.

## Test plan

- [x] Suite **1451 → 1476**, 0 fail (25 new)
- [x] `git diff --check` clean
- [x] All five touched/added modules pass `node --check`
- [x] Route smoke: degrades to `{ok:false, configured:false}` with no Blob store rather than throwing
- [x] `deploy-bundle` guard still green with the new `lib/research/` files
- [ ] CI green

## Known limits — stated, not hidden

- **Nothing is graded yet.** `research/decisions/` is empty until the first `?log=1` cron run writes a snapshot, and the earliest swing outcome resolves 5 sessions after that. There is a real waiting period before this produces any number — which is the honest state, and better than a grader that would happily emit one today.
- Grading is **single-horizon**, at each prediction's own intended horizon. The multi-horizon 1/3/5/10/21/63 vector remains unbuilt.
- **No sector benchmark** is wired, so residuals are market-relative only.

## Deployment note

`op=researchgrade` is **not** called by the warm cron — it runs only when invoked manually. Given the prior incident where that cron's tail silently died at the 55s ceiling, placement deserves its own thought rather than a blind append.

Shadow only — no change to live ranking.

items.title: Fix LoCoMo runner: ContextBuilder.build takes token_budget, packet has event_ids
items.body:
Two bugs in `benchmarks/locomo/run.py` that killed the first Voyage LoCoMo run:

- `composer.build(q.text, max_tokens=budget)` — `ContextBuilder.build`'s keyword is `token_budget=`, not `max_tokens=`. TypeError on the first question of the first conversation.
- `packet.events` — `ContextPacket` has `.event_ids` (tuple[str, ...]), not `.events`. The `hasattr(packet, 'events')` shield hid this by always returning `[]`; the split-measurement `final_context_ids` column would have been silently empty.

Both bugs date from PR #18 (LoCoMo scaffold). The local run I did on 2026-08-09 caught these and I fixed them but the fix was reset-hard away when the namespace-rename branch (#20) started. This commit restores the fix on main so the Voyage run Peter is asking for can actually execute.

## Additive

Benchmark scaffold only. No test change needed (LoCoMo smoke test doesn't exercise the final-context path).

items.title: Migrate PR #25 Grid tests and benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

- migrate all Grid-related Rust test surfaces from `PupilTong/lynx#25`, including 230 source layout tests, one W3C boundary regression, generated matrices, standalone/public wrappers, algorithm inventories, and Rust-only head-to-head scenarios
- migrate all 18 Grid-tagged benchmark scenarios into the `grid_pr25` CodSpeed target
- extend the shared generic test host for Grid without dynamic dispatch or styling-engine integration
- fix Grid intrinsic track sizing, cross-axis feedback, and positioned-item edge cases exposed by the migrated suite
- keep CSS Grid's final container-size/percentage pass independent from the bounded row↔column contribution corrections, with initial column probes using only definite-max row sizes per Grid §12.1

## Why

The high-performance Grid implementation is now on `main`, but the upstream PR #25 Grid coverage and workloads were not yet represented in neutron-star. This brings those regression tests and performance scenarios across while keeping head-to-head execution entirely in Rust; no Lynx C++ runner or styling-engine storage is included.

The migrated cross-axis measurement cases also exposed a pass-ordering bug: the previous minimal fix skipped final Grid sizing after an internal contribution correction. The W3C algorithm treats these as independent phases. This PR now preserves the final percentage-resolution pass and derives pre-row block-axis availability from definite max row tracks instead of the whole container height.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --check -p lynx-template-decoder -p lynx-widget -p stylo-dom -p neutron-star`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p neutron-star --locked --quiet`

### [`v1.6.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v160--2026-07-29)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.5.1...v1.6.0)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance (123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings)

##### New API — `Append`

```go
// Append to an array without knowing its length
data, _ = jsonparser.Append(data, []byte(`"new_item"`), "items")
```

- **`Append(data, value, keys...)`** — appends `value` to the end of the JSON array addressed by `keys`. Addresses the top-level value when `keys` is empty; auto-vivifies a missing keyed path as a single-element array. Returns `MalformedArrayError` when the addressed value is not an array. Traced to SYS-REQ-009, SYS-REQ-110.

##### Known issues — all resolved (zero open)

- **KI-2 fixed** — `ParseInt("-")` now returns an error instead of `(0, nil)`. One-line sign-only guard in `bytes.go:parseInt` (after stripping the sign byte, an empty remainder returns `(0, false, false)`).
- **KI-3 fixed** — `Set` with an array-index path component under an object parent (and vice-versa) now auto-coerces the container type instead of emitting malformed JSON. (Disposition already set to `fixed` in v1.5.x.)
- **KI-4 fixed** — `Set` on a top-level array-index beyond length now appends at the array's end (matching nested-array behavior under SYS-REQ-110) instead of returning `KeyPathNotFoundError`. Also cleans up trailing commas in malformed arrays.

**Zero open known issues.** Every previously shipped known issue is now resolved and covered by ReqProof L3 Assurance.

***

### [`v1.5.1`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v151--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.5.0...v1.5.1)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance (123 requirements, 0 errors, 0 warnings)

##### Performance — 6.1x large-payload speedup

- **Fix stringEnd unbounded backslash scan** — `stringEndConfig` was scanning the ENTIRE remaining parent document for backslashes (`bytes.IndexByte(data, '\\')`) instead of just the string body. On a 24kb large payload this walked tens of KB per string. Now bounded to `data[:firstQuote]` (the string body only). **128µs → 22µs (5.8x).**
- **SWAR string scan** — replaced two separate `bytes.IndexByte` calls (quote + backslash) with a single inline 8-byte SWAR (SIMD-Within-A-Register) loop that checks for both characters simultaneously. **22µs → 21µs (additional 8%).**

### [`v1.5.0`](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/blob/HEAD/CHANGELOG.md#v150--2026-07-28)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/compare/v1.4.0...v1.5.0)

##### Covered by [ReqProof](https://reqproof.com) — L3 Assurance

v1.5.0 extends the formal-verification coverage to **123 requirements** (0 errors, 0 warnings) across all new APIs. Every new function is traced via source annotations, tested with MC/DC witnesses, and covered by the structure-aware fuzzer.

##### Config struct — opt-in lenient parsing ([#​160](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/160), [#​115](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/115))

```go
var Lenient = jsonparser.Config{AllowSingleQuotes: true, AllowUnknownEscapes: true}
Lenient.Get(data, "key")  // parses {'key':'value'} and unknown escapes
```

- **`AllowSingleQuotes`** — accept `'key':'value'` alongside `"key":"value"` (JavaScript/Python-style). The same escape rules apply inside single-quoted strings.
- **`AllowUnknownEscapes`** — pass through unknown escape sequences (`` \` ``, `\x`) literally instead of erroring.
- The default Config is strict (RFC 8259 only). Package-level functions are unchanged.
- Config methods mirror the full API: `Get`, `GetString`, `Set`, `Delete`, `ArrayEach`, `ObjectEach`.

##### Streaming ReaderParser ([#​132](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/132), [#​257](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/257))

```go
rp := jsonparser.NewReaderParser(file)  // any io.Reader
rp.Get("users", "[0]", "name")          // path-based access from a stream
```

- Path-based access to JSON data from an `io.Reader` — **no need to load the entire document into memory**.
- Buffers data incrementally in 64KB chunks; memory is bounded by the largest value, not the document size.
- Enables parsing **10GB+ JSON files** without OOM.
- Methods: `Get`, `GetString`, `ArrayEach`.

##### Name aliases ([#​66](https://redirect.github.com/buger/jsonparser/issues/66))

| `EachObject`        | `ObjectEach`          |
| `EachArrayErr`      | `ArrayEachErr`        |
| `EachArrayWildcard` | `ArrayEachWildcard`   |

`EachKey`, `EachKeyErr`, `EachKeyWildcard` already matched the pattern. All old names remain functional.
